Complex exponential integral means spectra of univalent functions and the Brennan conjectureThanks: The author was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 11501157).
Jianjun Jin
Address: School of Mathematics, Hefei University of Technology, Xuancheng Campus, Xuancheng 242000, P.R.China
Email address: jin@hfut.edu.cn, jinjjhb@163.com
Abstract.
In this paper we investigate the complex exponential integral means spectra of univalent functions in the unit disk. We show that all integral means spectrum (IMS) functionals for complex exponents on the universal Teichmüller space, the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve, and the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space are continuous. We also show that the complex exponential integral means spectrum of any univalent function admitting a quasiconformal extension to the extended complex plane is strictly less than the universal integral means spectrum. These extend some related results in our recent work [39]. Here we employ a different and more direct approach to prove the continuity of the IMS functional on the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space. Additionally, we completely determine the integral means spectra of all univalent rational functions in the unit disk. As a consequence, we show that the Brennan conjecture is true for this class of univalent functions. Finally, we present some remarks and raise some problems and conjectures regarding IMS functionals on Teichmüller spaces, univalent rational functions, and a multiplication operator whose norm is closely related to the Brennan conjecture.
Key words and phrases: Complex exponential integral means spectrum of univalent function, universal integral means spectrum, Brennan conjecture, univalent function with a quasiconformal extension, univalent rational function, univalent polynomial, universal Teichmüller space, universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, universal Teichmüller curve
2020 Mathematics Subject ClassificationPrimary 30C55; Secondary 30C62

1. Introduction
Let  $\Delta=\{z:|z|<1\}$  be the unit disk in the complex plane  $\mathbb{C}$ . We denote by  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$  the extended complex plane and let  $\mathbb{R}$  be the real line.
For a complex number  $z$ , we use  $\arg z$  to denote the unique argument of  $z$  satisfying that  $\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi]$ . Let  $\Omega$  be a bounded simply connected domain in  $\mathbb{C}$  with  $0\in\Omega$ . Let  $f$  be an analytic function in  $\Omega$  with  $f(0)=1$  and  $f(z)\neq 0$  for all  $z\in\Omega$ . In this paper, we always use  $\log f$  to denote the unique single-valued branch of the logarithm of  $f$  in  $\Omega$  with  $\arg f(0)=0$ .
We denote by  $\mathcal{U}$  the class of all univalent functions (conformal mappings) in  $\Delta$ . We let  $\mathcal{S}$  be the class of all univalent functions  $f$  in  $\Delta$  with  $f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)-1=0$  and let  $\mathcal{S}_{b}$  be the subclass of  $\mathcal{S}$  which consists of all bounded univalent functions.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ . The integral means spectrum  $\beta_{f}(\tau)$  for  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  is defined as
(1.1)
$\beta_{f}(\tau):=\limsup_{r\rightarrow 1^{-}}\frac{\log\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}|d\theta}{|\log(1-r)|}.$
Remark 1.1.
For  $f\in\mathcal{S}$ , since  $f^{\prime}(z)$  is never zero in  $\Delta$  and  $f^{\prime}(0)=1$ , we define the complex power  $[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}$  as
$[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}=\exp(\tau\log f^{\prime}(z)).$
For real  $\tau$ , the integral means measure the boundary expansion and compression associated with a given conformal map. Allowing  $\tau$  to be a complex exponent, we should also take into account the rotation.
The universal integral means spectra  $B(\tau)$  and  $B_{b}(\tau)$  are defined as
$B(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}}\beta_{f}(\tau)\,\,\textup{and}\,\,B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{b}}\beta_{f}(\tau).$
Because of its important relation to the fine properties of harmonic measures in the complex plane, see [45], the universal integral means spectra of univalent functions have been studied extensively in recent years. It is an important and difficult problem to find out the exact values of the universal integral means spectra  $B(\tau)$  and  $B_{b}(\tau)$ . We shall first review some main known results and open problems for real  $\tau$  in this topic. It was first observed by Makarov in [45] that
Theorem 1.2.
$B(\tau)=\max\{B_{b}(\tau),3\tau-1\},\,\tau\in\mathbb{R}.$
For large  $\tau$ , Feng and MacGregor proved in [24] that  $B(\tau)=3\tau-1,\,\,\tau\geq\frac{2}{5}.$  Also for large  $\tau$ , see [50], we have  $B_{b}(\tau)=\tau-1,\,\,\tau\geq 2.$  By considering the lacunary series, Kayumov showed in [41] that
$B(\tau)>\frac{\tau^{2}}{5},\,\,0<\tau\leq\frac{2}{5}.$  In the paper [18], after establishing an important result in the theory of harmonic measures, Carleson and Makarov obtained that
Theorem 1.3.
There is a constant  $\tau_{*}<0$  such that
$B_{b}(\tau)=B(\tau)=|\tau|-1,\,\,\tau\leq\tau_{*}.$
It is only known that  $\tau_{*}\leq-2$ .
It is conjectured that  $\tau_{*}=-2$ . This is equivalent to the celebrated Brennan conjecture that  $B(-2)=B_{b}(-2)=1$ , which was raised in [16]. There have been many studies on the Brennan conjecture, see for example, [14], [15], [8], [29], [30], [33], [54], [56]. The current best upper bound estimate about  $B(-2)$  is provided by Hedenmalm and Shimorin in [33]. In the paper [17], Carleson and Jones conjectured that  $B_{b}(1)=\frac{1}{4}$ . A more generalized conjecture was given by Kraetzer in [42] that
Conjecture 1.4.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ . Then
$B_{b}(\tau)=\begin{cases}\frac{\tau^{2}}{4},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\,\tau\in[-2,2],\\
|\tau|-1,\;\text{if}\;\,\tau\in(-\infty,-2)\cup(2,+\infty).\end{cases}$
For the complex exponents  $\tau$ , there are only several known results about  $B(\tau)$  and  $B_{b}(\tau)$ . In an unpublished preprint [12], Binder extended Makarov’s Theorem 1.2 to the complex setting.
Theorem 1.5.
(1) If  $\textup{Re}(\tau)>0$ , then  $B(\tau)=\max\{B_{b}(\tau),|\tau|+2\textup{Re}(\tau)-1\}.$
(2) If  $\textup{Re}({\tau})\leq 0$ , then  $B(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau)$ .
In a 1987 paper [10], Becker and Pommerenke extended the Brennan conjecture to the complex case, asking whether  $B_{b}(\tau)=1$  whenever  $|\tau|=2$ . Baranov and Hedenmalm proved in [7] that
Theorem 1.6.
$B_{b}(2-\tau)\leq 1-\textup{Re}(\tau)+[\frac{9e^{2}}{2}+o(1)]|\tau|^{2}\log\frac{1}{|\tau|},\,\,\,\textup{as}\,\,\,|\tau|\rightarrow 0.$
Binder continued to study the integral means spectrum in [13] for complex exponents and proved the following
Theorem 1.7.
For each  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ , there exists  $T_{\theta}>0$  such that  $B_{b}(te^{i\theta})=t-1$  for  $t\geq T_{\theta}$ .
Also in [13], Binder conjectured that the following generalization of Kraetzer’s conjecture still holds.
Conjecture 1.8.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ . Then
$B_{b}(\tau)=\begin{cases}\frac{\tau^{2}}{4},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\,|\tau|<2,\\
|\tau|-1,\;\text{if}\;\,|\tau|\geq 2.\end{cases}$
More known results on the universal integral means spectrum and related topics can be found in the monograph [27, Chapter VIII] and recent survey [32] given by Hedenmalm and Sola.
From the fractal approximation principle(see [45] and [17]), we have
Theorem 1.9.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , we have
$B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}}\beta_{f}(\tau).$
Remark 1.10.
Here,  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  is the class of all univalent functions  $f$  that belong to  $\mathcal{S}_{b}$  and admit a quasiconformal extension to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ . In the rest of the paper, when a univalent function  $f$  belongs to  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$ , we will still use  $f$  to denote its quasiconformal extension.
There have been some studies on the integral means spectra of univalent functions admitting a quasiconformal extension, see for example [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [51] and [52].
From Theorem 1.9, we can see the problem that determining the exact values of  $B_{b}(\tau)$  as a global extremal problem in the class  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$ . To enrich the understanding of the theory of integral means spectra of univalent functions, in the present paper, we continue to consider the following problem, which differs from previous studies that finding a better estimation for  $B_{b}(\tau)$ .
Problem 1.11.
(1) For fixed  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ ,
what topology can be endowed upon the class  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  such that the integral means spectrum  $\beta_{f}(\tau)$  is continuous on  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$ ?
(2) For given  $\tau\neq 0$ , does there exist at least one extremal function for  $B_{b}(\tau)$ ? (3) If the extremal functions for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  exist, in which subset of  $\mathcal{S}$  do they lie?
Here and later, we say a function  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  is an extremal function for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  if  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau)$ . In the recent work [39], we have studied Problem 1.11 for real  $\tau$ . It has been pointed out that the functional  $I:f\rightarrow\beta_{f}(\tau),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ , is not continuous on  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  under the locally uniformly convergence topology, see [39, Remark 5.8]. In [39], we introduced and studied the integral means spectrum (IMS) functionals on the Teichmüller spaces. It has been proved in [39] that all IMS functionals on the universal Teichmüller space, the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve, and the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space are continuous. It was also shown in [39] that the real exponential integral means spectrum of any univalent function admitting a quasiconformal extension to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  is strictly less than the universal integral means spectrum. This result means that, for  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ , the extremal functions for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  cannot be from the class  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$ . The first main purpose of this paper is to extend these results to the complex setting. We shall prove that
Theorem 1.12.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{{T}}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau),\,\,[\mu]_{T}\in{T},$
is continuous.
Theorem 1.13.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{{AT}}:[\mu]_{AT}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau),\,\,[\mu]_{AT}\in{AT},$  is continuous.
Theorem 1.14.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau),\,\,\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}},$  is continuous.
Theorem 1.15.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ . Then we have  $\beta_{f}(\tau)<B_{b}(\tau)$  for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ .
The rest of paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we will fix some notations used in this paper and recall some basic properties about univalent functions, quasiconformal mappings, and the definitions of quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. Also, Theorem 1.12-1.15 will be restated in Section 2. We will provide some lemmas in Section 3. We shall give the proof of Theorem 1.12 and 1.13 in Section 4. We will prove Theorem 1.14 and 1.15 in Section 5. In Section 6, we study the integral means spectra of univalent rational functions in  $\Delta$  and prove that the Brennan conjecture is true for this class of functions. We also check that the Brennan conjecture holds for any univalent function from the unit disk onto the interior of a bounded polygon. In Section 7, for IMS functionals on Teichmüller spaces, univalent rational functions, and a multiplication operator whose norm is closely related to the Brennan conjecture, we finally present some remarks and raise some problems and conjectures.
2. Preliminaries and restatement of the first main results
In this section, we first fix some notations that will be used later, and then recall some basic definitions and properties of univalent functions(conformal mappings), quasiconformal mappings, and quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. For the main references, see [20, 47, 43, 44] and [5, 25, 21, 23, 22, 43, 58].
We let  $\Delta^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\Delta}$  be the exterior of  $\Delta$  and let  $\mathbb{T}=\partial\Delta=\partial\Delta^{*}$  to be the unit circle. We let  $\mathcal{A}(\Delta)$  denote the class of all analytic functions in  $\Delta$ . We use the notation  $\Delta(r)$  to denote the disk centered at  $0$  with radius  $r$ . For two compact sets  $X,Y$  of the complex plane, we define the distance of  $X$  and  $Y$ , denoted by  ${\text{dist}}\{X,Y\}$ , as
${\textup{dist}}\{X,Y\}:=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}|x-y|.$
Let  $\Omega$  be a simply connected proper subdomain of  $\mathbb{C}$ . We shall use  $\rho_{\Omega}$  to denote the hyperbolic metric with curvature  $-4$  in  $\Omega$ . That is  $\rho_{\Omega}(w)=|g^{\prime}(w)|/({1-|g(w)|^{2}}),\,\,w\in\Omega.$
Here  $g$  is a univalent function from  $\Omega$  to  $\Delta$ . In particular,  $\rho_{\Delta}(z)=(1-|z|^{2})^{-1},z\in\Delta.$
2.1. Univalent functions and quasiconformal mappings
It is well known that
Proposition 2.1.
Let  $f\in\mathcal{U}$ . Then, for any  $z\in\Delta$ ,
${\textup{dist}}(f(z),\partial f(\Delta))\leq(1-|z|^{2})|f^{\prime}(z)|\leq 4{\textup{dist}}(f(z),\partial f(\Delta)).$
We let  ${E}_{j}$  be the Banach space of functions  $\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta)$  with the norm
$\|\phi\|_{E_{j}}:=\sup_{z\in\Delta}|\phi(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{j}<\infty,\,\,\,\,j=1,2.$
Let  $f$  be a locally univalent function in an open domain  $\Omega$  of  $\mathbb{C}$ . The Pre-Schwarzian derivative  $N_{f}$  of  $f$ , and the Schwarzian derivative  $S_{f}$  of  $f$  are defined as
$N_{f}(z):=\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(z)}{{f^{\prime}(z)}},\,z\in\Omega,$
and
$S_{f}(z):=[N_{f}(z)]^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2}[N_{f}(z)]^{2}=\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(z)}{f^{\prime}(z)}-\frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(z)}{f^{\prime}(z)}\right]^{2},\,z\in\Omega.$
Let  $g$  be another locally univalent function in  $f(\Omega)$ . Then we have
(2.1)
$N_{g\circ f}(z)=N_{g}(f(z))[f^{\prime}(z)]+N_{f}(z),\,\,z\in\Omega,$
and
(2.2)
$S_{g\circ f}(z)=S_{g}(f(z))[f^{\prime}(z)]^{2}+S_{f}(z),\,\,z\in\Omega.$
It is well known that
$|N_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})\leq 6\,\,{\text{and}}\,\,|S_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{2}\leq 6,$
for all  $f\in\mathcal{U}$ . This means that
$\|N_{f}\|_{E_{1}}\leq 6\,\,{\text{and}}\,\,\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}\leq 6$  for any  $f\in\mathcal{U}$ . We define the classes  $\mathbf{N}$  and  $\mathbf{S}$  as
$\mathbf{N}=\{\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\,\phi=N_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}\},$
and
$\mathbf{S}=\{\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\,\phi=S_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}\}.$
Then  $\mathbf{N}\subset E_{1}$  and  $\mathbf{S}\subset E_{2}$ . Moreover, we have
Proposition 2.2.
$\mathbf{N}$  and  $\mathbf{S}$  are closed in  $E_{1}$  and  $E_{2}$ , respectively.
We say a sense-preserving homeomorphism  $f$ , from an open domain  $\Omega$  in
$\mathbb{C}$  to another one, is a quasiconformal mapping if it has locally square
integral distributional derivatives and satisfies the Beltrami equation  $\bar{\partial}f=\mu_{f}\partial{f}$  with
$\|\mu_{f}\|_{\infty}=\mathop{\text{ess sup}}\limits_{z\in\Omega}|\mu_{f}(z)|<1.$
Here the function  $\mu_{f}(z)$  is called the Beltrami coefficient of  $f$  and
$\bar{\partial}f=f_{\bar{z}}:=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)f,$
$\partial f=f_{z}:=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}-i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)f.$
Let  $f$  be a quasiconformal mapping from one open domain  $\Omega_{1}$  to another domain  $\Omega_{2}$ . If  $g$  is another quasiconformal mapping from  $\Omega_{1}$  to  $\Omega_{3}$ . Then the Beltrami coefficients of  $f$  and  $g\circ f^{-1}$  satisfy the following chain rule.
(2.3)
$\mu_{g\circ f^{-1}}\circ f(z)=\frac{1}{\chi}\frac{\mu_{g}(z)-\mu_{f}(z)}{1-\overline{\mu_{f}(z)}\mu_{g}(z)},\,\,\chi=\frac{\overline{\partial f}}{\partial f},\,\,\,z\in\Omega_{1}.$
Let  $f$  be a bounded univalent function in a Jordan domain  $\Omega$  of  $\mathbb{C}$  admitting a quasiconformal extension (still denoted by  $f$ ) to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ . The boundary dilatation of  $f$ , denoted by  $b(f)$ , is defined as
(2.4)
$b(f):=\inf\{\|\mu_{f}|_{\Omega^{*}-E}\|_{\infty}:\,E{\text{ is a compact set in}}\,\,\Omega^{*}\}.$
Here  $\Omega^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\Omega}$  is seen as an open set in the Riemann sphere  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  under the spherical distance and  $b(f)$  is the infimum of  $\|\mu_{f}|_{\Omega^{*}-E}\|_{\infty}$  over all compact subsets  $E$  contained in  $\Omega^{*}$ .
2.2. Quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces
Let  $\Omega$  be a bounded Jordan domain in  $\mathbb{C}$  with  $0\in\Omega$ , and let  $\Omega^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\Omega}$ .
We use  $M(\Omega^{*})$  to denote the open unit ball of the Banach space  $L^{\infty}({\Omega}^{*})$  of essentially bounded measurable functions in  ${\Omega}^{*}$ . For  $\mu\in M({\Omega}^{*})$ , let  $f_{\mu}$  be the quasiconformal mapping in the extended complex plane  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  with complex dilatation equal to  $\mu$  in  $\Omega^{*}$ , equal to  $0$  in  $\Omega$ , normalized  $f_{\mu}(0)=0,\,f^{\prime}_{\mu}(0)=1,\,f_{\mu}(\infty)=\infty$ . We say two elements  $\mu$  and  $\nu$  in  $M(\Omega^{*})$  are equivalent, denoted by  $\mu\sim\nu$ , if  $f_{\mu}|_{\Omega}=f_{\nu}|_{\Omega}$ . The equivalence class of  $\mu$  is denoted by  $[\mu]_{T(\Omega)}$ . Then  $T(\Omega)=M(\Omega^{*})/\sim$  is one model of Teichmüller space of the domain  $\Omega$ .
For any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\Omega^{*})$ , we let
$\sigma(\mu,\nu)(\zeta):=\frac{\mu(\zeta)-\nu(\zeta)}{1-{\overline{\nu(\zeta)}}\mu(\zeta)},\,\zeta\in\Omega^{*}.$
The (hyperbolic) distance  $d_{\Omega}(\mu,\nu)$  of two elements  $\mu,\nu$  in  $M(\Omega^{*})$  is defined as
$d_{\Omega}(\mu,\nu):=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}}{1-\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}}=\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}.$
The Teichmüller distance  $d_{T}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)})$  of two points  $[\mu]_{T(\Omega)}$ ,  $[\nu]_{T(\Omega)}$  in  $T(\Omega)$  is defined as
$\displaystyle d_{T}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\sim\mu,\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\sim\mu,\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}}{1-\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}}\Big\}.$
We say  $\mu$  and  $\nu$  in  $M({\Omega}^{*})$  are asymptotically equivalent, denoted by  $\mu\approx\nu$ , if there exists  $\widetilde{\nu}$  in  ${M}(\Omega^{*})$  such that  $[\widetilde{\nu}]_{T(\Omega)}=[{\nu}]_{T(\Omega)}$  and  $\widetilde{\nu}(\zeta)-{\mu}(\zeta)\rightarrow 0$  as  $\textup{dist}(\zeta,\partial\Omega)\rightarrow 0^{+}$ . The asymptotic equivalence
of  $\mu$  will be denoted by  $[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)}$ . The asymptotic Teichmüller space  $AT(\Omega)$  is the set of
all asymptotic equivalence classes  $[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)}$  of elements  $\mu$  in  $M({\Omega}^{*})$ . The Teichmüller distance  $d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)})$  of two points  $[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)}$ ,  $[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)}$  in  $AT(\Omega)$  is defined as
$\displaystyle d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))}{1-h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))}\Big\}.$
Here, for  $\mu\in M(\Omega^{*})$ ,  $h^{*}(\mu)$  is defined as
(2.5)
$h^{*}(\mu)=\inf\{\|\mu|_{\Omega^{*}-E}\|_{\infty}:\,E{\text{ is a compact set in}}\,\,\Omega^{*}\}.$
Remark 2.3.
We note that  $h^{*}(\mu)=b(f_{\mu})$  for  $\mu\in M(\Omega^{*})$ , here  $b(f_{\mu})$  is defined as in (2.4).
Remark 2.4.
We shall mainly consider the Teichmüller spaces defined on  $\Delta$ . We next will use  $T$ ,  $AT$  to denote  $T(\Delta)$ ,  $AT(\Delta)$ , respectively.  $T$  and  $AT$  are known as universal Teichmüller space and universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, respectively. For the sake of simplicity, the equivalence classes  $[\mu]_{T(\Delta)}$  and  $[\mu]_{AT(\Delta)}$  will be denoted by  $[\mu]_{T}$  and  $[\mu]_{AT}$ , respectively.
Remark 2.5.
Note that for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ , we can find a  $\mu\in M(\Delta^{*})$  such that  $f=\sigma\circ f_{\mu}$ ,  $\sigma$  is a Möbius transformation. Then we check from Theorem 1.9 that
$B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{{[\mu]_{T}}\in T}\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)$
for each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ .
2.3. Restatement of the first main results
We will study the following IMS functional defined on  $T$  and prove that
Theorem 2.6 (=Theorem 1).
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{{T}}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)$  on  $T$  is continuous.
For the IMS functional on the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, we shall show that
Theorem 2.7 (=Theorem 2).
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{{AT}}:[\mu]_{AT}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)$  is well-defined and continuous on  $AT$ .
We set
$\mathcal{T}:=\{\phi:\phi=N_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}\}.$
$\mathcal{T}$  is seen as one model of universal Teichmüller curve, see [11, 55]. It is known that  $\mathcal{T}$  is an open connected subset of  $E_{1}$ , see [58]. Since  $\mathbf{N}$  is closed in  $E_{1}$ , then the closure  $\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  of  $\mathcal{T}$  is contained in  $\mathbf{N}$ . We view  $\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  as a model for the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve.
For any  $\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ , there is a unique univalent function  $f_{\phi}(z)$  with  $f_{\phi}\in\mathcal{S}$  and such that
$\phi(z)=N_{f_{\phi}}(z).$  Actually, we can take
(2.6)
$f_{\phi}(z)=\int_{0}^{z}e^{\int_{0}^{\zeta}\phi(w)dw}d\zeta,\,\,\,z\in\Delta.$
We shall prove that
Theorem 2.8 (=Theorem 3).
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)$  is continuous on  $\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ .
Also, we will prove the following result, which indicates that the IMS functional on the class  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  satisfies the maximum modulus principle.
Theorem 2.9 (=Theorem 4).
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ . Then we have  $\beta_{f}(\tau)<B_{b}(\tau)$  for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ .
3. Five lemmas
In this section, we will recall three known lemmas and establish two new ones. First, we will use the following criterion for the integral means spectrum, see [32], [33], [54].
We define the Hilbert space  $\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)$  as
$\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)=\{\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\|\phi\|_{\alpha}^{2}:=(\alpha+1)\iint_{\Delta}|\phi(z)|^{2}(1-|z|^{2})^{\alpha}\frac{dxdy}{\pi}<\infty\}.$
Then
Lemma 3.1.
Let  $\alpha>-1$ . For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , we have
$\beta_{f}(\tau)=\inf\{\alpha+1:\,\,[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau/2}\in\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)\}.$
We need the following result, which is a special case of Proposition 2.14 in [39].
Lemma 3.2.
Let  $f$  belong to  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  with  $f(\infty)=\infty$ . Let  $\mathbf{h}$  be a bounded univalent function in  $f(\Delta)$  with  $\mathbf{h}(0)=\mathbf{h}^{\prime}(0)-1=0$ . We assume that  $\mathbf{h}$  admits a quasiconformal extension (still denoted by  $\mathbf{h}$ ) to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  with  $\mathbf{h}(\infty)=\infty$  and  $b(\mathbf{h})=0$ . Then, for any  $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{3}(1-\|\mu_{f}\|_{\infty}))$ , there are two constants  $C(f,{\bf{h}})>0$ ,  $\delta>0$  such that
$|N_{\mathbf{h}}(\zeta)|{\textup{dist}}(\zeta,f(\mathbb{T}))<C(f,\mathbf{h})\varepsilon,$
for all  $\zeta\in f(\Delta)$  with  ${\textup{dist}}(\zeta,f(\mathbb{T}))<\delta$ .
We will use the following lemma.
Lemma 3.3.
Let  $f$  belong to  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  with  $f(\infty)=\infty$ . Assume that  $\mathbf{h}$  is a bounded univalent function in  $\Omega:=f(\Delta)$  with  $\mathbf{h}(0)=\mathbf{h}^{\prime}(0)-1=0$  and admits a quasiconformal extension (still denoted by  $\mathbf{h}$ ) to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  with  $\mathbf{h}(\infty)=\infty$ . Then we have
(3.1)
$|N_{\mathbf{h}}(\zeta)|\rho_{\Omega}^{-1}(\zeta)\leq 8\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty},$
for all  $\zeta\in\Omega$ .
Remark 3.4.
This lemma can be proved by the arguments in the proof of Proposition 3.3 in [39].
The following two lemmas are also needed.
Lemma 3.5.
Let  $f,g\in\mathcal{S}$  and let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ . If there is a constant  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$\sup\limits_{|z|\in(r_{0},1)}|N_{g}(z)-N_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon,$
for some positive number  $\varepsilon$ . Then there exist two positive numbers  $C_{1}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)$  and  $C_{2}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)$  such that
$C_{1}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)\Big(\frac{1-|z|}{1+|z|}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}}\leq|[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}|\leq C_{2}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)\Big(\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}},$
for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ . Here  $\mathbf{h}=g\circ f^{-1}$ .
Proof.
In view of  $\mathbf{h}=g\circ f^{-1}$ , we obtain from (2.1) that
$N_{g}(z)-N_{f}(z)=\frac{{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)}{{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)}\cdot f^{\prime}(z).$
Let
$G(z):=\frac{{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)}{{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)}\cdot f^{\prime}(z),\,\,H(z):={\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z).$
It is easy to see that
$\log[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}=\tau\log H(z)\,\,\textup{and}\,\,[\log H(z)]^{\prime}=G(z).$
Let  $z=|z|e^{i\arg z}$  be such that  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ , then
(3.2)
$\log[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}=\tau\log H(z)=\tau\int_{z_{0}}^{z}G(\zeta)d\zeta+\tau\log H(z_{0}),$
here,  $z_{0}=r_{0}e^{i\arg z}$  and the integral is taken on the radial path from  $z_{0}$  to  $z$ .
On the other hand, note that
$|G(z)(1-|z|^{2})|<\varepsilon,$
for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ , hence we obtain that
(3.3)
$\displaystyle\Big|\int_{z_{0}}^{z}G(\zeta)d\zeta\Big|$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\Big|\int_{r_{0}}^{|z|}G(te^{i\arg z})e^{i\arg z}dt\Big|$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\Big|\int_{r_{0}}^{|z|}G(te^{i\arg z})(1-t^{2})\cdot\frac{e^{i\arg z}}{1-t^{2}}dt\Big|$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle\int_{r_{0}}^{|z|}\frac{\varepsilon}{1-t^{2}}dt=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Big[\log\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}-\log\frac{1+r_{0}}{1-r_{0}}\Big].$
We denote
$\mathbf{M}_{0}=\max\limits_{|z|=r_{0}}|\log H(z)|=\max\limits_{|z|=r_{0}}|\log{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)|.$
Then, from the fact  $\Big|\log|[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}|\Big|\leq\Big|\log[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}\Big|$ , and (3.2), (3.3), we get that
$\Big|\log|[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}|\Big|\leq\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}\Big[\log\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}-\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}\Big]+|\tau|\mathbf{M}_{0},$
for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ . It follows that
$e^{-|\tau|\mathbf{M}_{0}}\Big(\frac{1+r_{0}}{1-r_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}}\Big(\frac{1-|z|}{1+|z|}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}}\leq|[{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}|\leq e^{|\tau|\mathbf{M}_{0}}\Big(\frac{1-r_{0}}{1+r_{0}}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}}\Big(\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}\Big)^{\frac{|\tau|\varepsilon}{2}},$
for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ . This proves the lemma.
∎
Lemma 3.6.
Let  $f,g\in\mathcal{S}$  and let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ . (1) If  $\beta_{f}(\tau):=\beta>0$ , and there is a constant  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$\sup\limits_{|z|\in(r_{0},1)}|N_{g}(z)-N_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon/|\tau|,$
for  $\varepsilon\in(0,\beta)$ , then we have
$|\beta_{g}(\tau)-\beta_{f}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon.$
(2) If  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=0$ , and there is a constant  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$\sup\limits_{|z|\in(r_{0},1)}|N_{g}(z)-N_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon/|\tau|,$
for  $\varepsilon>0$ , then we have  $\beta_{g}(\tau)\leq\varepsilon$ .
Proof.
(1) Let  $\mathbf{h}=g\circ f^{-1}$ . First, by Lemma 3.5, we have
(3.4)
$C_{1}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)\Big(\frac{1-|z|}{1+|z|}\Big)^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\leq|{\mathbf{h}}^{\prime}\circ f(z)|\leq C_{2}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)\Big(\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}\Big)^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}},$
for  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ . On the other hand, since  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=\beta>0$ , we see from Lemma 3.1 that, for  $\varepsilon\in(0,\beta)$ ,
(3.5)
$\iint_{\Delta}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta+\varepsilon/2}dxdy<\infty,$
and
(3.6)
$\iint_{\Delta}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta-\varepsilon/2}dxdy=\infty.$
Hence it follows from the second inequality of (3.4) and (3.5) that
$\displaystyle\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[g^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta+\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle=\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}||[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta+\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle\leq[C_{2}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)]\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}\Big(\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}\Big)^{\varepsilon/2}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta+\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle\leq 2^{\varepsilon}[C_{2}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)]\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta+\varepsilon/2}dxdy<\infty.$
Then it is easy to see from Lemma 3.1 that  $\beta_{g}(\tau)\leq\beta+\varepsilon.$  Also, from the first inequality of (3.4) and (3.6), we have
$\displaystyle\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[g^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta-\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle=\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)]^{\tau}||[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta-\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle\geq[C_{1}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)]\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}\Big(\frac{1-|z|}{1+|z|}\Big)^{\varepsilon/2}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta-\varepsilon}dxdy$
$\displaystyle\geq 2^{-\varepsilon}[C_{1}(r_{0},\tau,\varepsilon)]\iint_{\Delta-\Delta(r_{0})}|[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}|(1-|z|^{2})^{-1+\beta-\varepsilon/2}dxdy=\infty.$
This implies that  $\beta_{g}(\tau)\geq\beta-\varepsilon$ . Hence we have  $|\beta_{g}(\tau)-\beta|\leq\varepsilon$ . This proves (1) of Lemma 3.6.
(2) When  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=0$ , for  $\varepsilon>0$ , repeating the above arguments by only using the second inequality of (3.4) and (3.5), we can prove that  $\beta_{g}(\tau)\leq\varepsilon.$  This proves (2) of Lemma 3.6 and the proof of Lemma 3.6 is done. ∎
4. Proof of Theorem 1.12 and 1.13
Note that  $d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})\leq d_{T}([\mu]_{T},[\nu]_{T})$  for any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , we see that the statement that  $I_{AT}$  is continuous on  $AT$  implies Theorem 1.12. Hence we only need to prove Theorem 1.13. By studying the Pre-Schwarzian derivative model of the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, we have proved in [39] that Theorem 1.13 holds for real  $\tau$ . We will use a more direct way to show that Theorem 1.13 holds for all complex numbers  $\tau$ . More precisely, we will prove Theorem 1.13 by using some arguments from the theory of Teichmüller spaces and some results from the extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings.
4.1. Isomorphism mapping between Teichmüller spaces
We first recall some arguments from the theory of quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. For a fixed  $\omega\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , let  $\mathbf{\Omega}:=f_{\omega}(\Delta)$  and  $\mathbf{\Omega}^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\mathbf{\Omega}}$ . For any  $\mu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , we define
$\sharp(\mu)(\zeta):=\mu_{f_{\mu}\circ f_{\omega}^{-1}}(\zeta)=\Big[\frac{1}{\chi}\frac{\mu-\omega}{1-\overline{\omega}\mu}\Big]\circ f_{\omega}^{-1}(\zeta),\,\,\zeta\in\mathbf{\Omega}^{*}.$
Here  $\chi=\frac{\overline{\partial f_{\omega}}}{\partial f_{\omega}}$ . We will next write  $\mu^{\sharp}(\zeta)=\sharp(\mu)(\zeta)$ . Then, from  $f_{\mu}=f_{\mu^{\sharp}}\circ f_{\omega}$ , we obtain
$\mu(z)=\mu_{f_{\mu^{\sharp}}\circ f_{\omega}}(z)=\frac{{\omega}(z)+(\mu^{\sharp}\circ f_{\omega}(z))\chi}{1+\overline{\omega(z)}(\mu^{\sharp}\circ f_{\omega}(z))\chi},\,\,z\in\Delta^{*}.$
This means that the mapping  $\sharp:\mu(z)\mapsto\mu^{\sharp}(\zeta)$  is one-to-one from  $M({\Delta}^{*})$  to  $M({\mathbf{\Omega}}^{*})$  and, for any  $\nu\in M({\mathbf{\Omega}}^{*})$ ,
$\sharp^{-1}(\nu)(z)=\frac{{\omega}(z)+(\nu\circ f_{\omega}(z))\chi}{1+\overline{\omega(z)}(\nu\circ f_{\omega}(z))\chi},\,\,\chi=\frac{\overline{\partial f_{\omega}}}{\partial f_{\omega}},\,\,z\in\Delta^{*}.$
We shall write  ${}^{\sharp}\nu(z)=\sharp^{-1}(\nu)(z)$  for  $\nu\in M({\mathbf{\Omega}}^{*}).$  Meanwhile, it is easy to see that the mapping  $\dagger:[\mu(z)]_{T}\mapsto[\mu^{\sharp}(\zeta)]_{T(\bf{\Omega})}$  is one-to-one from  $T$  to  $T({\mathbf{\Omega}})$ .
By a direct computation, for any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , we have
(4.1)
$\left|\sigma(\mu,\nu)(z)\right|=\left|\frac{\mu^{\sharp}-\nu^{\sharp}}{1-{\overline{\nu^{\sharp}}\mu^{\sharp}}}\circ f_{\omega}(z)\right|=\left|\sigma(\mu^{\sharp},\nu^{\sharp})(\zeta)\right|,\,\zeta=f_{\omega}(z),\,z\in\Delta^{*}.$
Similarly, for any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\bf{\Omega}^{*})$ , we have
(4.2)
$\left|\sigma(\mu,\nu)(\zeta)\right|=\left|\frac{{}^{\sharp}\mu-{{}^{\sharp}}\nu}{1-{\overline{{}^{\sharp}\nu}{{}^{\sharp}}\mu}}\circ f_{\omega}^{-1}(\zeta)\right|=\sigma({{}^{\sharp}}\mu,{{}^{\sharp}}\nu)(z),\,z\in\Delta^{*},\,\zeta=f_{\omega}(z).$
It follows that
$\displaystyle d_{T}([\mu]_{T},[\nu]_{T})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\sim\mu,\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}^{\sharp}\sim\mu^{\sharp},\nu_{1}^{\sharp}\sim\nu^{\sharp}}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1}^{\sharp},\nu_{1}^{\sharp})\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle d_{T}([\mu^{\sharp}]_{T(\mathbf{\Omega})},[\nu^{\sharp}]_{T(\mathbf{\Omega})}).$
We have shown that
Proposition 4.1.
The mapping  $\dagger:[\mu(z)]_{T}\mapsto[\mu^{\sharp}(\zeta)]_{T(\mathbf{\Omega})}$  is an isometric isomorphism from  $T$  to  $T({\mathbf{\Omega}})$ .
It is known that
Proposition 4.2.
Let  $\Omega$  be a bounded Jordan domain in  $\mathbb{C}$  with  $0\in\Omega$ . Let  $\mu,\nu\in M({\Omega}^{*})$ . Then  $\mu\approx\nu$  in  $M({\Omega}^{*})$ , if and only if there exist  $\widetilde{\mu}$ ,  $\widetilde{\nu}$  in  $M({\Omega}^{*})$  such that  $\widetilde{\mu}\sim\mu$ ,  $\widetilde{\nu}\sim\nu$  and  $\widetilde{\mu}(\zeta)-\widetilde{\nu}(\zeta)\rightarrow 0$  as  $\textup{dist}(\zeta,\partial{\Omega})\rightarrow 0$ .
If  $\mu\approx\nu$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$ , then, by Proposition 4.2, there exist  $\widetilde{\mu}$ ,  $\widetilde{\nu}$  in  $M({\Delta}^{*})$  such that  $\widetilde{\mu}\sim\mu$ ,  $\widetilde{\nu}\sim\nu$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$  and  $\widetilde{\mu}(z)-\widetilde{\nu}(z)\rightarrow 0$  as  $|z|\rightarrow 1^{+}$ . It follows from (4.2) that  $\widetilde{\mu}^{\sharp}(\zeta)-\widetilde{\nu}^{\sharp}(\zeta)\rightarrow 0$  as  $\textup{dist}(\zeta,\partial{\bf{\Omega}})\rightarrow 0$ . From Proposition 4.1, we see that  $\widetilde{\mu}^{\sharp}\sim\mu^{\sharp}$ ,  $\widetilde{\nu}^{\sharp}\sim\nu^{\sharp}$  in  $M(\bf{\Omega}^{*})$ . By Proposition 4.2 again, we obtain that  $\mu^{\sharp}\approx\nu^{\sharp}$  in  $M(\bf{\Omega}^{*})$ . Similarly, by using Proposition 4.2, Lemma 4.1 and (4.1), we can show that  $\mu\approx\nu$  in  $M(\bf{\Omega}^{*})$  implies that  ${{}^{\sharp}}\mu\approx{{}^{\sharp}}\nu$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$ . Moreover, for any  $\mu,\nu$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$ , we have
$\displaystyle d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}^{\sharp}\approx\mu^{\sharp},\nu_{1}^{\sharp}\approx\nu^{\sharp}}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1}^{\sharp},\nu_{1}^{\sharp})\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle d_{AT}([\mu^{\sharp}]_{T(\mathbf{\Omega})},[\nu^{\sharp}]_{T(\mathbf{\Omega})}).$
We have shown that
Proposition 4.3.
The mapping  ${\ddagger}:[\mu(z)]_{AT}\mapsto[\mu^{\sharp}(\zeta)]_{AT(\mathbf{\Omega})}$  is an isometric isomorphism from  $AT$  to  $AT({\mathbf{\Omega}})$ .
Remark 4.4.
In particular, for  $\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , we see that
$\nu\approx\omega$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$  if and only if  ${\nu}^{\sharp}\approx 0$  in  $M(\mathbf{\Omega}^{*})$ , and
$d_{AT}([\omega]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})=d_{AT}([0]_{AT(\mathbf{\Omega})},[\nu^{\sharp}]_{AT(\mathbf{\Omega})}).$
4.2. Extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings
We recall some definitions and results on the extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings. For a bounded Jordan domain  $\Omega$  in  $\mathbb{C}$  with  $0\in\Omega$ , let  $\mu\in M(\Omega)$ . We define
$k_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\{\|\nu\|_{\infty}:\nu\sim\mu\},$
and
$h_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\{h^{*}(\nu):{\nu}\sim\mu\}.$
Here  $h^{*}(\nu)$  is defined as in (2.5). It is obvious that  $h_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})\leq k_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})$ . We say  $[\mu]_{T}$  is a Strebel point if  $h_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})<k_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})$ , otherwise, it is called a non-Strebel point.
Let
$H_{0}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)})=\inf\{h^{*}(\nu):{\nu}\approx\mu\}.$
It is known that  $H_{0}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)})=h_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})$ . We say some  $\widetilde{\mu}\in[\mu]_{AT({\Omega})}$  is non-Strebel extremal in  $[\mu]_{AT({\Omega})}$  if it satisfies that  $H_{0}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)})=h_{0}([\widetilde{\mu}]_{T(\Omega)})=k_{0}([\widetilde{\mu}]_{T(\Omega)})=\|\widetilde{\mu}\|_{\infty}$ . It is easy to see that  $H_{0}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)})=h_{0}([\widetilde{\mu}]_{T(\Omega)})=k_{0}([\widetilde{\mu}]_{T(\Omega)})=h^{*}(\widetilde{\mu})=\|\widetilde{\mu}\|_{\infty}$ , if  $\widetilde{\mu}$  is non-Strebel extremal in  $[\mu]_{AT({\Omega})}$ . From [57, Lemma 4.1], we know that
Proposition 4.5.
For any  $\mu\in M({{\Omega}}^{*})$ , there always exists some  $\widetilde{\mu}$  which is non-Strebel extremal in  $[\mu]_{AT({{\Omega}})}$ .
4.3. A claim
Let  $\Omega$  be a bounded Jordan domain in  $\mathbb{C}$  with  $0\in\Omega$ . For any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\Omega^{*})$ , we let
${{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)}):=\inf\limits_{{\mu_{1}\sim\mu},\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))\|_{\infty}\Big\},$
${\bf{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)}):=\inf\limits_{{\mu_{1}\approx\mu},\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))\|_{\infty}\Big\}.$
We first note that
${{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\limits_{{\mu_{1}\sim\mu}}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu))\|_{\infty}\Big\},$
so that
${\bf{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\limits_{{\mu_{1}\approx\mu}}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu))\|_{\infty}\Big\}.$
Also, for any  $\nu_{1},\nu_{2}$  with  $\nu_{1}\approx\nu_{2}$  in  $M(\Omega^{*})$ , we observe that
${\bf{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu_{1}]_{T(\Omega)})={\bf{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu_{2}]_{T(\Omega)}).$
It follows that
(4.3)
$\displaystyle d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\bf{d}}^{*}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu))\|_{\infty}\Big\}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|h^{*}(\sigma(\mu,\nu_{1}))\|_{\infty}\Big\}.$
Now, given fixed  $\omega\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , let still  $\mathbf{\Omega}=f_{\omega}(\Delta)$  and  $\mathbf{\Omega}^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\mathbf{\Omega}}$ . For any  $\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , let  $\widehat{{\nu}}$  be non-Strebel extremal in  $[{\nu}^{\sharp}]_{AT(\mathbf{\Omega})}$ , and let  $d:=d_{AT}([\omega]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})$ . Then from (4.3) and Proposition 4.5, we have
$d_{AT}([0]_{AT(\bf{\Omega)}},[\nu^{\sharp}]_{AT(\bf{\Omega})})=d_{\bf{\Omega}}(0,\widehat{{\nu}})=\tanh^{-1}\|\widehat{{\nu}}\|_{\infty}.$
On the other hand, from Remark 4.4 of Proposition 4.3, we know that
$d=d_{AT}([\omega]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})=d_{AT}([0]_{AT(\bf{\Omega)}},[\nu^{\sharp}]_{AT(\bf{\Omega})})=\tanh^{-1}\|\widehat{{\nu}}\|_{\infty}.$
Consequently, from (4.2), we have
$d_{\Delta}(\omega,\widetilde{\nu})=d_{\bf{\Omega}}(0,\widehat{{\nu}})=\tanh^{-1}\|\widehat{{\nu}}\|_{\infty}=d,$
so that
$d=d_{\Delta}(\omega,\widetilde{\nu})=\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\omega,\widetilde{\nu})\|_{\infty}.$
Here  $\widetilde{\nu}={{}^{\sharp}}\widehat{{\nu}}\in[\mu]_{AT}$ , and  $f_{\widetilde{\nu}}=f_{\widehat{{\nu}}}\circ f_{\omega}$ . Replace  $\omega$  by  $\mu$  in the above arguments, we obtain that
Claim 4.6.
For any  $\mu,\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , let  $d:=d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})$ . Then there is a  $\widetilde{\nu}\in[\nu]_{AT}$  such that  $d=d_{\Delta}(\mu,\widetilde{\nu})=\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma({\mu},\widetilde{\nu})\|_{\infty},$
and  $b({\mathbf{h}})=\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}$ . Here,  $\mathbf{h}=f_{\widetilde{\nu}}\circ f_{\mu}^{-1}$ .
4.4. Proof of Theorem 1.13
We shall first prove the following result, which implies that the IMS functional  $I_{AT}$  is well-defined.
Proposition 4.7.
Let  $\mu,\nu\in{M}({\Delta}^{*})$ . For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , if  $\mu\approx\nu$  in  ${M}({\Delta}^{*})$ , then  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)$ .
Remark 4.8.
In particular,  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=0$  for any  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  if  $\mu\approx 0$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$ . We call  $f_{\mu}$  is an asymptotically conformal mapping in  $\Delta$  when  $\mu\approx 0$  in  $M(\Delta^{*})$ . In general, we say a function  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{b}$  is an asymptotically conformal mapping in  $\Delta$  if it admits a quasiconformal extension (still denoted by  $f$ ) to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  with  $\mu_{f}(z)\rightarrow 0$  as  $|z|\rightarrow 1^{+}$ , see [26], [48], [49]. From Proposition 4.7, we see that
$B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{[\mu]_{AT}\in AT}\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)$
for each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ .
Proof of Proposition 4.7.
The case  $\tau=0$  is obvious, we will only consider  $\tau\neq 0$ . When  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=\beta>0$ .
Since  $\mu\approx\nu$ , then we know there is a  $\widetilde{\nu}$  such that  $\widetilde{\nu}\sim\nu$  in  ${M}({\Delta}^{*})$  and  $\mu(z)-\widetilde{\nu}(z)\rightarrow 0$  as  $|z|\rightarrow 1^{+}$ . Let  $\mathbf{h}=f_{\widetilde{\nu}}\circ f_{\mu}^{-1}$ . Then from (2.3), we see that  $b(\mathbf{h})=0$ . It follows from Lemma 3.2 and Proposition 2.1 that
$\displaystyle\|N_{f_{\mu}}(z)-N_{f_{\nu}}(z)\|_{E_{1}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\|N_{f_{\mu}}(z)-N_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(z)\|_{E_{1}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle|(N_{\mathbf{h}}\circ f_{\mu}(z))|\cdot|f^{\prime}_{\mu}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle 4|(N_{\mathbf{h}}\circ f_{\mu}(z))|\textup{dist}(f_{\mu}(z),f_{\mu}(\mathbb{T}))\rightarrow 0,\,\,{\text{a}s}\,\,\,|z|\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Hence, for any  $\varepsilon\in(0,\beta)$ , there is an  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$\sup\limits_{|z|\in(r_{0},1)}|N_{f_{\mu}}(z)-N_{f_{\nu}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon/|\tau|.$
From (1) of Lemma 3.6, we obtain that  $|\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon.$  This means that  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)$ .
When  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=0$ . For any  $\varepsilon>0$ , by using (2) of Lemma 3.6, we can similarly prove that  $\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)\leq\varepsilon.$  This implies that  $\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)=0$ .
The proposition is proved.
∎
We proceed to prove Theorem 1.13. First, it is easy to see that Theorem 1.13 holds for  $\tau=0$ . We next will assume that  $\tau\neq 0$ . For any  $\mu\in M(\Delta^{*})$ , we first consider the case when  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=\beta>0$ . To prove the functional  $I_{AT}$  is continuous on  $[\mu]_{AT}$ , it suffices to show that, for any small  $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a positive constant  $\delta>0$  such that
$|\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon,$
for all  $[\nu]_{AT}$  with  $d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})<\delta.$
For given  $\mu\in{M}(\Delta^{*})$ , let  $\nu\in M(\Delta^{*})$  with  $d:=d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})$ . Then,
from Claim 4.6, we know that there is a  $\widetilde{\nu}\in[\nu]_{AT}$  such that  $d=d_{\Delta}(\mu,\widetilde{\nu})=\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma({\mu},\widetilde{\nu})\|_{\infty},$
and  $b({\mathbf{h}})=\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}$ . Here,  $\mathbf{h}=f_{\widetilde{\nu}}\circ f_{\mu}^{-1}$ . It follows that
$b(\mathbf{h})=\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}=\|\sigma({\mu},\widetilde{\nu})\|_{\infty}=\tanh d\leq d,$
and
$N_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(z)-N_{f_{\mu}}(z)=N_{\mathbf{h}}\circ f_{\mu}(z)\cdot f_{\mu}^{\prime}(z),\,z\in\Delta.$
Then, by using Lemma 3.3 with respect to  $f_{\mu}$  and  $\mathbf{h}$ , we see that
$\displaystyle\sup\limits_{z\in\Delta}|N_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(z)-N_{f_{\mu}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})$
$\displaystyle=\sup\limits_{z\in\Delta}|N_{\mathbf{h}}\circ f_{\mu}(z)|\cdot|f_{\mu}^{\prime}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})$
$\displaystyle=\sup\limits_{\zeta\in f_{\mu}(\Delta)}|N_{\mathbf{h}}(\zeta)|\rho_{f_{\mu}(\Delta)}^{-1}(\zeta)\leq 8\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}.$
Consequently, for any small  $\varepsilon>0$ , we take  $\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{8|\tau|}$ , then, when
$d=d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})<\delta,$
we obtain that  $\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}=b(\bf{h})<\delta$  and
$\displaystyle\sup\limits_{z\in\Delta}|N_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(z)-N_{f_{\mu}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})\leq 8\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}<\varepsilon/|\tau|.$
It follows from (1) of Lemma 3.6 that
$|\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)|=|\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon.$
This proves the functional  $I_{AT}$  is continuous on  $[\mu]_{AT}$  when  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)>0$ .
We now consider the case when  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=0$ . For any small  $\varepsilon>0$ , by using the same arguments above, we still take  $\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{8|\tau|}$ , then, when  $d=d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})<\delta$ , we can obtain that
$\|\mu_{\mathbf{h}}\|_{\infty}<\delta$  and so that
$\displaystyle\sup\limits_{z\in\Delta}|N_{f_{\widetilde{\nu}}}(z)-N_{f_{\mu}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon/|\tau|,$
Hence from (2) of Lemma 3.6, we have  $\beta_{f_{\nu}}(\tau)\leq\varepsilon$ . This implies that  $I_{AT}$  is continuous on  $[\mu]_{AT}$  in this case. The proof of Theorem 1.13 is complete.
5. Proof of Theorem 1.14 and 1.15
5.1. Proof of Theorem 1.14
Since  $\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)=0$  for any  $M(\Delta^{*})$  when  $\tau=0$ , then, obviously, Theorem 1.14 holds for the case  $\tau=0$ . So we will assume that  $\tau\neq 0$ . For any  $\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ , we will take  $f_{\phi}$  as in (2.6). For given  $\psi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ . When  $\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)=\beta>0$ , to prove  $I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}$  is continuous at the point  $\psi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ , it suffices to prove that, for small  $\varepsilon>0$ , we can find a constant  $\delta>0$  such that  $|\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon,$
for any  $\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  with  $\|\phi-\psi\|_{E_{1}}<\delta$ .
Actually, for any  $\varepsilon\in(0,\beta)$ , we can take  $\delta=\varepsilon/|\tau|$ . Now, we assume that  $\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  satisfy that  $\|\phi-\psi\|_{E_{1}}<\delta=\varepsilon/|\tau|$ . Then we can choose a constant  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$\sup\limits_{|z|\in(r_{0},1)}|N_{f_{\phi}}(z)-N_{{f}_{\psi}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})<\varepsilon/|\tau|.$
Consequently, by (1) of Lemma 3.6, we obtain that  $|\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)-\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)|\leq\varepsilon.$
This proves that  $I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}$  is continuous at the point  $\psi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  when  $\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)>0$ .
When  $\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)=0$ , for any  $\varepsilon>0$ , we still take  $\delta=\varepsilon/|\tau|$ . Similarly, by using (2) of Lemma 3.6, we can obtain that  $\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)\leq\varepsilon$  for any  $\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  with  $\|\phi-\psi\|_{E_{1}}<\delta$ . This implies that  $I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}$  is continuous at the point  $\psi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}$  when  $\beta_{f_{\psi}}(\tau)=0$ . Now, we finish the proof of Theorem 1.14.
5.2. Proof of Theorem 1.15
To prove Theorem 1.15, we first show the following result.
Proposition 5.1.
Let  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ . If  $\beta_{f}(\tau_{0})>0$  for some  $\tau_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ , then the function  $\gamma(t):=\beta_{f}(\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0})$ ,  $t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}=[0,+\infty)$  is strictly increasing on  $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ .
Remark 5.2.
Let  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ . From Proposition 5.1, we easily see that, for any fixed  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the function  $\gamma_{\tau}(t):=\beta_{f}(\tau+t\tau)$
is nondecreasing on  $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ .
Proof.
We let  $\beta_{f}(\tau_{0})=\beta>0$ . Let  $\varepsilon<\beta$  be a positive number, which will be fixed later. Then we see from the definition of integral means spectrum of  $f$  that
there is a sequence  $\{{\bf r}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$  with  ${\bf r}_{n}<1$  and  ${\bf r}_{n}\rightarrow 1$  as  $n\rightarrow\infty$ , and such that
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta>(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta-\varepsilon)}.$
We set
$\mathbf{A}_{n}:=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta,\,\,\mathbf{D}_{n}:=(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta-\varepsilon)},\,\,n\in\mathbb{N},$
and define
${\mathbf{E}}_{n}:=\{\theta:|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|>\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi},\,\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\},$
$\mathbf{F}_{n}:=\{\theta:|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\leq\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi},\,\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\}.$
It is obvious that  $\mathbf{E}_{n}\bigcup\mathbf{F}_{n}=(-\pi,\pi]$  and  $\mathbf{E}_{n}\bigcap\mathbf{F}_{n}=\emptyset.$  We denote
$\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{E}}=\int_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta,\,\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{F}}=\int_{\mathbf{F}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta.$
Then we see that  $\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{E}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\bf{A}_{n}$  or  $\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{F}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\bf{A}_{n}$ .
Case I. If  $\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{E}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\bf{A}_{n}$ , then, for any  $t>0$ , we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\cdot|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|^{t}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\cdot|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|^{t}d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle\Big(\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi}\Big)^{t}\int_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi}\Big)^{t}\mathbf{A}_{n}$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 2^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}[\mathbf{D}_{n}]^{1+t}.$
That is
(5.1)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 2^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}{(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta-\varepsilon)(1+t)}}.$
Case II. If  $\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{F}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{A}_{n}$ , we set
$\mathbf{G}_{n}:=\{\theta:|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\leq\frac{1}{8}\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi},\,\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\},$
${\mathbf{H}_{n}}:=\{\theta:\frac{1}{8}\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi}<|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\leq\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi},\,\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\}.$
We easily see that  $\mathbf{G}_{n}\bigcup\mathcal{H}_{n}=\mathbf{F}_{n}$  and  $\mathbf{G}_{n}\bigcap\mathbf{H}_{n}=\emptyset.$  Then we have
$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{H}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{F}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta-\int_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{A}_{n}-2\pi\frac{1}{8}\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{2\pi}$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\frac{3}{8}\mathbf{D}_{n}.$
Consequently, we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\cdot|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|^{t}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{H}_{n}}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|\cdot|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}}|^{t}d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle\frac{3}{8}\mathbf{D}_{n}\left(\frac{\mathbf{D}_{n}}{16\pi}\right)^{t}$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 16^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}[\mathbf{D}_{n}]^{1+t}.$
Therefore,
(5.2)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 16^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}{(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta-\varepsilon)(1+t)}}.$
Thus, it follows from (5.1) and (5.2) that
(5.3)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 16^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}{(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta-\varepsilon)(1+t)}}.$
Now, for any  $t>0$ , we take  $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\beta t}{1+t}\in(0,\beta)$ , so that
$(\beta-\varepsilon)(1+t)=\beta+\frac{1}{2}\beta t.$
Hence, we see from (5.3) that
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}({\bf r}_{n}e^{i\theta})]^{\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0}}|d\theta$
$\displaystyle>$
$\displaystyle 16^{-1-t}\pi^{-t}{(1-{\bf r}_{n})^{-(\beta+\frac{1}{2}\beta t)}}.$
This implies that
$\beta_{f}(\tau_{0}+t\tau_{0})\geq\beta+\frac{1}{2}\beta t>\beta=\beta_{f}(\tau_{0}).$
Proposition 5.1 is proved.
∎
We next finish the proof of Theorem 1.15. For  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ ,  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ . First, it is easy to see that Theorem 1.15 obviously holds if  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=0$ . Hence we next assume that  $\beta_{f}(\tau)>0$  for some  $\tau\neq 0$ .
We define a locally univalent function  $\mathbf{h}$  on the domain  $\Omega:=f(\Delta)$  as
$\mathbf{h}(w)=\int_{0}^{w}[f^{\prime}(\mathbf{g}(\zeta))]^{\varepsilon}d\zeta,\,\,w\in f(\Delta).$
Here  $\mathbf{g}=f^{-1}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$  is a small number. Then,  ${\bf{h}}(0)={\bf{h}}^{\prime}(0)-1=0$  and
(5.4)
$\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)=[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\varepsilon},z\in\Delta,$
and
(5.5)
$\mathbf{h}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)\cdot f^{\prime}(z)=\varepsilon[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\varepsilon-1}f^{\prime\prime}(z),z\in\Delta.$
It follows from (5.4) and (5.5) that
$\frac{\mathbf{h}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)}{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)}\cdot f^{\prime}(z)=\varepsilon N_{f}(z),\,z\in\Delta,$
so that
$\displaystyle|N_{\mathbf{h}}(w)|\rho_{\Omega}^{-1}(w)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\Big|\frac{\mathbf{h}^{\prime\prime}(w)}{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}(w)}\Big|\frac{1-|\mathbf{g}(w)|^{2}}{|\mathbf{g}^{\prime}(w)|}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\Big|\frac{\mathbf{h}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)}{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)}\Big|\cdot|f^{\prime}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})=\varepsilon|N_{f}(z)|\rho_{\Delta}^{-1}(z)\leq 6\varepsilon.$
Set  $\mathbf{F}(z)=\mathbf{h}\circ f(z),z\in\Delta$ . We see that
$\|N_{\bf F}(z)-N_{f}(z)\|_{E_{1}}=|N_{\mathbf{h}}(w)|\rho_{\Omega}^{-1}(w)\leq 6\varepsilon.$
Hence we see from [9], [5] or [58] that  $\mathbf{F}$  is bounded univalent in  $\Delta$  and admits a quasiconformal extension to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  when  $\varepsilon$  small enough. Now, we let  $\varepsilon$  small enough so that  $\mathbf{F}$  belongs to  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$ . On the other hand, we note that, for any  $r\in(0,1),\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,
$\displaystyle[\mathbf{F}^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle[\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}\cdot[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\varepsilon\tau}\cdot[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}=[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau+\varepsilon\tau}.$
Thus we have  $\beta_{\mathbf{F}}(\tau)$ = $\beta_{f}(\tau+\varepsilon\tau)$ . It follows from Proposition 5.1 that  $\beta_{\mathbf{F}}(\tau)>\beta_{f}(\tau)$ , so that  $\beta_{f}(\tau)<B_{b}(\tau)$  for all  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$  when  $\beta_{f}(\tau)>0$ . The proof of Theorem 1.15 is finished.
Remark 5.3.
Note that for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ , there is always an  $F\in\mathcal{S}$  such that  $N_{F}=\phi\in\partial\mathcal{T}$  and  $\phi=aN_{f},a>1$ . We let  $\mathbf{h}=F\circ f^{-1}$ . Then  $\mathbf{h}$  is univalent in  $f(\Delta)$  and
$(a-1)N_{f}=N_{F}(z)-N_{f}(z)=\frac{\mathbf{h}^{\prime\prime}\circ f(z)}{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z)}\cdot f^{\prime}(z).$
Integrate both sides of the above equation from  $0$  to  $z$ , we obtain that
$(a-1)\log f^{\prime}(z)=\log\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z).$
Hence  $\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(z))=[f^{\prime}(z)]^{a-1}$ . It follows that for any  $r\in(0,1),\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,
$\displaystyle[F^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle[\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\circ f(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}\cdot[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}=[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{a\tau},\tau\in\mathbb{C}.$
From Remark 5.2, we have  $\beta_{F}(\tau)=\beta_{f}(a\tau)\geq\beta_{f}(\tau)$ . This implies that
$\sup_{\phi\in\partial\mathcal{T}}\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)\geq\sup_{\phi\in\mathcal{T}}\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau).$
On the other hand, from Theorem 1.5, we know that  $B(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau)$  if  ${\text{Re}}(\tau)\leq 0$ . Hence we have
$B_{b}(\tau)\geq\sup_{\phi\in\partial\mathcal{T}}\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)$
when  ${\text{Re}}(\tau)\leq 0$ . We have checked that
Corollary 5.4.
If  ${\text{Re}}{(\tau)}\leq 0$ , then  $B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{\phi\in\partial{\mathcal{T}}}\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau).$
6. Integral means spectra of the univalent rational functions
In this section, we study the integral means spectra of univalent rational functions in the unit disk  $\Delta$ . Since directly studying the integral means spectrum of univalent rational functions in  $\Delta$  is inconvenient, we enlarge the scope to the general class of locally univalent functions in  $\Delta$ . The locally univalent functions allow for the definition of a generalized integral means spectrum, see (6.11) below. In particular, this generalized spectrum coincides with the classical one for the univalent rational functions. We then completely determine the generalized integral means spectra for a certain class of locally functions, thereby proving that univalent rational functions in the unit disk satisfy the Brennan conjecture. We also check that the Brennan conjecture is true for any univalent function from the unit disk onto the interior of a bounded polygon.
In the rest of the paper, the notation  $P_{n}(z)$  denotes a polynomial of degree  $n$ ,  $n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ . In particular,  $P_{n}$  is a complex constant when  $n=0$ . We denote by  $\mathcal{R}$  the class of all rational functions  $R$  in  $\Delta$  with  $R(0)=R^{\prime}(0)-1=0$  and which have no poles in  $\Delta$ . Let  $\Omega$  be a subset of the complex plane. If  $R$  is analytic in  $\Omega$ , we say  $R$  has no zeros, or one zero in  $\Omega$  if the equation  $R(z)=0$  has no roots, or one root in  $\Omega$ , respectively. If  $R$  is analytic in  $\Omega\setminus\Omega_{1}$ ,  $\Omega_{1}$  is a finite (or empty) subset of  $\Omega$ , we will say  $R$  has no critical points, or one critical point in  $\Omega$ , if there is no point  $z\in\Omega$ , or one point  $z\in\Omega$  such that  $R$  is analytic in  $z$  and  $R^{\prime}(z)=0$ , respectively. A rational function  $R\in\mathcal{R}$  can be uniquely represented as
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}=\frac{z+a_{2}z^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}z^{n}}{1+b_{1}z+\cdots+b_{m}z^{m}}.$
Here,  $P_{n}$  and  $P_{m}$  have no common factors except 1 and  $P_{m}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\Delta$ .
6.1. Certain locally univalent functions and the main result of this section
We use  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$  to denote the class of all univalent rational functions  $R$  belonging to  $\mathcal{R}$ .
We denote by  $\mathcal{U}_{P}$  the class which consists of all univalent polynomials contained in  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . It is easy to see that  $\mathcal{U}_{P}$  is contained in  $\mathcal{S}_{b}$ . It should be pointed out that the univalent polynomials are dense in  $\mathcal{S}$ , see [20] or [2]. This fact is one of the reasons for our investigation of the classes  $\mathcal{U}_{P}$  and  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . When  $R(z)$  belongs to  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ , we know from the Koebe distortion theorem that
$|R(z)|\leq\frac{|z|}{(1-|z|)^{2}}.$
In view of this fact, we shall consider the following three classes of rational functions contained in  $\mathcal{R}$ .
Definition 6.1.
${\bullet}$  Class  ${\mathcal{L}_{I}}$ . The class  ${\mathcal{L}_{I}}$  consists of all functions  $R\in\mathcal{R}$  that can be written as
(6.1)
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}.$
Here,  $P_{n}$  and  $P_{m}$  have no common factors except  $1$ , and  $P_{m}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}=\Delta\cup\mathbb{T}$ . It is easy to see that  $\mathcal{U}_{P}\subset\mathcal{L}_{I}.$
${\bullet}$  Class  ${\mathcal{L}_{II}}$ . The class  ${\mathcal{L}_{II}}$  consists of all functions  $R\in\mathcal{R}$  that can be written as
(6.2)
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})P_{m}(z)}.$
Here,  $P_{m}$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ ,  $l\in\mathbb{N},\theta_{j}\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,  $\theta_{j_{1}}\neq\theta_{j_{2}}$  whenever  $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ , the numerator and denominator of  $R$  have no common factors except  $1$ .
${\bullet}$  Class  ${\mathcal{L}_{III}}$ . The class  ${\mathcal{L}_{III}}$  consists of all functions  $R\in\mathcal{R}$  that can be written as
(6.3)
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{2}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})P_{m}(z)}.$
Here,  $P_{m}$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ ,  $l\in\mathbb{N},\theta_{j}\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,  $\theta_{j_{1}}\neq\theta_{j_{2}}$  whenever  $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ ,  $t\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ ,  $\widetilde{\theta}_{k}\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,  $\widetilde{\theta}_{k_{1}}\neq\widetilde{\theta}_{k_{2}}$  whenever  $k_{1}\neq k_{2}$ , and  ${\theta}_{j}\neq\widetilde{\theta}_{k}$  for all  $1\leq j\leq l,$   $1\leq k\leq t$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R$  have no common factors except  $1$ . In particular, the case  $t=0$  means that the denominator of  $R$  is  $\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{2}P_{m}(z).$
Remark 6.2.
We see that  $\mathcal{U}_{R}\subset\mathcal{L}_{I}\cup{\mathcal{L}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{L}_{III}}$ .
As we shall see later, the integral means spectra of functions  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  that have no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ , are different from those of functions  $R$  that have at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ . We will list some examples of univalent rational functions  $R(z)$  which has no critical points, or has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
We first consider the univalent polynomials.
Example 6.3.
Take  $P_{1}(z)=z$ , then  $P^{\prime}_{1}(z)=1$  so that  $P_{1}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.4.
Take  $P_{2}(z):=z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2}$ , then  $P^{\prime}_{2}(z)=1-z$  so that  $P_{2}$  has one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.5.
Take  $P_{3}(z):=z-\frac{1}{3}z^{3}$ , then  $P^{\prime}_{3}(z)=(1-z)(1+z)$  so that  $P_{3}$  has two critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.6.
Take  $P_{5}(z)=z-\frac{1}{6}z^{3}-\frac{1}{10}z^{5}$ , then  $P^{\prime}_{5}(z)=-\frac{1}{2}(z^{2}-1)(z^{2}+2)$  so that  $P_{5}$  has two critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  and two other ones not on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Remark 6.7.
$P_{1},P_{2},P_{3},P_{5}$  are all contained in  $\mathcal{U}_{P}\cap\mathcal{L}_{I}$ .
Next, we consider the univalent rational functions, which are unbounded in  $\Delta$ .
Example 6.8.
Take  $R_{1}(z)=\frac{z}{1-z},$  then  $R_{1}^{\prime}(z)=\frac{1}{(1-z)^{2}}$  so that  $R_{1}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.9.
Take  $R_{2}(z)=\frac{z^{2}+3z}{3(1-z)},$  then  $R_{2}^{\prime}(z)=-\frac{(z-3)(z+1)}{3(1-z)^{2}}$  so that  $R_{2}$  has one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.10.
Take  $R_{3}(z)=\frac{z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}},$  then  $R_{3}^{\prime}(z)=\frac{1}{(1-z)^{3}}$  so that  $R_{3}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Example 6.11.
Take  $R_{4}(z)=\kappa(z):=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{2}},$  here  $\kappa$  is the famous Koebe function, then  $R_{4}^{\prime}(z)=\frac{1+z}{(1-z)^{3}}$  so that  $R_{4}$  has one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Remark 6.12.
Both  $R_{1}$  and  $R_{2}$  belong to  $\mathcal{U}_{R}\cap\mathcal{L}_{II}$  while both  $R_{3}$  and  $R_{4}$  belong to  $\mathcal{U}_{R}\cap\mathcal{L}_{III}$ .
Remark 6.13.
When  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . If  $R$  has a critical point  $z_{1}$  on  $\mathbb{T}$ , because  $R$  is univalent, it follows that
$|R^{\prime}(z)|\geq\frac{1-|z|}{(1+|z|)^{3}}.$
Then  $R^{\prime}(z)$  must have the form
$R^{\prime}(z)=(z-z_{1})\frac{P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Here,  $P_{\bf n}$  and  $P_{\bf m}$  have no common factors except 1,  $P_{\bf n}(z_{1})\neq 0$ ,  $P_{\bf m}(z)=0$  has no zeros in  $\Delta$ .
Generally, if  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then  $R^{\prime}(z)$  can be written as the following unique form.
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Here,  $s\in\mathbb{N}$ , and  $z_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,s$  are all distinct critical points of  $R$  on  $\mathbb{T}$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R^{\prime}$  have no common factors except  $1$ .  $P_{\bf n}(z)$  has no zeros on  $\mathbb{T}$ , and  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\Delta$ .
Now, we introduce another subclass of  $\mathcal{R}$  as follows.
Definition 6.14.
For a function  $R\in\mathcal{R}$ , we say it belongs to the class  $\mathcal{R}_{O}$ , if  $R^{\prime}$  can be written uniquely in the following form:
(6.4)
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}:=\frac{\Pi(z)P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Here  $s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ . When  $s\geq 1$ ,  $z_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,s$  are all distinct critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  of  $R$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R^{\prime}$  have no common factors except  $1$ .  $P_{\bf n}(z)$  has no zeros on  $\mathbb{T}$ , and  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\Delta$ . The case  $s=0$  means that  $\Pi(z)\equiv 1$  and  $R$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Remark 6.15.
It is easy to see that  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$  is contained in  $\mathcal{R}_{O}\cap({\mathcal{L}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{L}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{L}_{III}}).$
Remark 6.16.
For  $R\in\mathcal{R}_{O}$ , we let, as in (6.4),
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Furthermore,
(a) If  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{R}_{O}\cap\mathcal{L}_{I}$ , we let, as in (6.1),
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}.$
Then
(6.5)
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{P^{\prime}_{n}(z)P_{m}(z)-P_{n}(z)P^{\prime}_{m}(z)}{[P_{m}(z)]^{2}}=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}$
Note that the numerator and denominator of the last rational function in (6.5) have no common factors except  $1$  so that  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}.$
(b) If  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{R}_{O}\cap\mathcal{L}_{II}$ , we let, as in (6.2),
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})P_{m}(z)}:=\frac{1}{\Pi_{1}}\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}.$
Then
(6.6)
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{\Pi_{1}[P^{\prime}_{n}(z)P_{m}(z)-P_{n}(z)P^{\prime}_{m}(z)]-\Pi_{1}^{\prime}P_{n}(z)P_{m}(z)}{\Pi_{1}^{2}[P_{m}(z)]^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\Pi_{1}^{2}P_{b}(z)}.$
Here, the numerator and denominator of the last rational function in (6.6) have no common factors except  $1$  so that  $P_{\bf m}(z)=\Pi_{1}^{2}P_{b}(z)=\Pi_{1}^{2}P_{{\bf m}-2l}(z)$ , and  $P_{b}(z)=P_{{\bf m}-2l}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ .
(c) If  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{R}_{O}\cap\mathcal{L}_{III}$ , we let, as in (6.3),
$R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{2}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})P_{m}(z)}:=\frac{1}{\Pi_{2}}\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}.$
Then
(6.7)
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{\Pi_{2}[P^{\prime}_{n}(z)P_{m}(z)-P_{n}(z)P^{\prime}_{m}(z)]-\Pi_{2}^{\prime}P_{n}(z)P_{m}(z)}{\Pi_{2}^{2}[P_{m}(z)]^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{b}(z)}.$
Here, the numerator and denominator of the last rational function in (6.7) have no common factors except  $1$  so that
$P_{\bf m}(z)=\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{b}(z)=\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{{\bf m}-3l-2t}(z),$
and  $P_{b}(z)=P_{{\bf m}-3l-2t}(z)$  has no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ .
Therefore, based on the above arguments, we next will consider the following subclasses  $\mathcal{Q}_{I}$ ,  $\mathcal{Q}_{II}$ ,  $\mathcal{Q}_{III}$  of the class of all locally univalent functions in  $\Delta$  for the purpose of the paper.
Definition 6.17.
Let  $R$  be a locally univalent function in  $\Delta$ , and it is analytic on  $\mathbb{T}$  except finitely many singular points.
$\bullet$  We say  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{I}$ , if  $R^{\prime}$  can be written in the following form
(6.8)
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}:=\frac{\Pi(z)P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)},\,z\in\overline{\Delta}.$
Here  $s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ . When  $s\geq 1$ ,  $z_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,s$  are all distinct critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  of  $R$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R^{\prime}$  have no common factors except  $1$ .  $P_{\bf n}(z)$  and  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  have no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ . The case  $s=0$  means that  $\Pi(z)\equiv 1$  and  $R$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
$\bullet$  We say  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{II}$ , if  $R^{\prime}$  can be written in the following form
(6.9)
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{2}P_{{\bf m}}(z)},\,z\in\overline{\Delta}.$
Here  $s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\},l\in\mathbb{N}$ . When  $s\geq 1$ ,  $z_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,s$  are all distinct critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  of  $R$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R^{\prime}$  in (6.9) have no common factors except  $1$ .  $P_{\bf n}(z)$  and  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  have no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ . In particular,  $R^{\prime}$  has no zeros on  $\mathbb{T}$  when  $s=0$ .
$\bullet$  We say  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{III}$ , if  $R^{\prime}$  can be written in the following form
(6.10)
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{\bf m}(z)},\,z\in\overline{\Delta}.$
Here  $s,t\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\},l\in\mathbb{N}$ . When  $s\geq 1$ ,  $z_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,s$  are all distinct critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  of  $R$ . The numerator and denominator of  $R^{\prime}$  in (6.10) have no common factors except  $1$ .  $P_{\bf n}(z)$  and  $P_{\bf m}(z)$  have no zeros in  $\overline{\Delta}$ . In particular,  $R^{\prime}$  has no zeros on  $\mathbb{T}$  when  $s=0$  and  $R^{\prime}$  has no
poles of order  $2$  on  $\mathbb{T}$  when  $t=0$ .
Remark 6.18.
We see that  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$  is contained in  ${\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}}.$
We will show the Brennan conjecture  $B(-2)=1$  is true for the class  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . Actually, we shall completely determine the generalized integral means spectra of functions belonging to the class  $({\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}})$  for all real  $\tau$ .
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$  and  $R$  be a locally univalent function in  $\Delta$ . We define the generalized integral means spectrum  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}$  of  $R$  as
(6.11)
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau):=\limsup\limits_{r\rightarrow 1^{-}}\frac{\log\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta}{|\log(1-r)|}.$
Remark 6.19.
Note that, for any  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ , this definition is the same as in (1.1) when  $R$  belongs to  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ .
We now present the main result of this section.
Theorem 6.20.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$  and let  $R\in({\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}})$ . Then
$(\bf A)$  when  $\tau=0$ , we have  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0$  for all  $R\in({\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}})$ ,
$(\bf B)$  when  $\tau<0$ , we have
$({\bf b_{1}})$  if  $R$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0$ ,
$({\bf b_{2}})$  if  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}0,\;\;\;\quad\,\,\,\,\text{for}\,\;\tau\in(-1,0),\\
|\tau|-1,\;\text{for}\,\;\tau\leq-1,\end{cases}$
$(\bf C)$  when  $\tau>0$ , we have
$({\bf c_{1}})$  if  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{I}$ , then  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0$ ,
$({\bf c_{2}})$  if  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{II}$ , then
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}2\tau-1,\;\text{for}\,\;\tau>\frac{1}{2},\\
0,\;\quad\quad\,\text{for}\,\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{2}],\end{cases}$
$({\bf c_{3}})$  if  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{III}$ , then
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}3\tau-1,\;\text{for}\,\;\tau>\frac{1}{3},\\
0,\;\quad\quad\,\text{for}\,\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{3}],\end{cases}$
Remark 6.21.
Since  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\beta_{R}(\tau)$  for all  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ ,  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ , as a direct consequence of Theorem 6.20, we have
Corollary 6.22.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$  and  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . Then all the statements  $(\bf A)$ ,  $(\bf B)$ , and  $(\bf C)$  in Theorem 6.20 hold.
In particular, we see from Corollary 6.22 that  $\beta_{R}(\tau)={\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)\leq|\tau|-1$  for all  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  when  $\tau\leq-2$ , which implies that
Corollary 6.23.
The Brennan conjecture  $B(-2)=1$  is true for the class  $\mathcal{U}_{R}$ .
6.2. Proof of Theorem 6.20
To prove Theorem 6.20, we need the following lemmas.
Lemma 6.24.
Let  $\varkappa\in\mathbb{R},r\in(0,1)$ . For any fixed  $\alpha\in(0,{\pi}]$ , we have
(1) when  $\varkappa>1$ ,
(6.12)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\asymp\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
(2) when  $\varkappa=1$ ,
(6.13)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\asymp\log\frac{1}{1-r},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
(3) when  $\varkappa<1$ ,
(6.14)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\asymp 1,\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Here and later, the notation  $A\asymp B$  for  $A>0,B>0$  means that there are two constants  $C_{1}>0,C_{2}>0$  such that  $C_{1}A\leq B\leq C_{2}A$ .
Remark 6.25.
This lemma seems to be known in the literature. For completeness, we will include a detailed proof for it.
Proof of Lemma 6.24.
We only prove case (1) when  $\varkappa>1$ , the other two cases can be shown similarly.
We first prove the case  $\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ . Recall that, for  $\theta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ ,
(6.15)
$1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2}\leq\cos\theta\leq 1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{4}.$
For  $\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ , we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}=\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1+r^{2}-2r\cos\theta|^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}.$
By (6.15), we obtain that
(6.16)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\leq\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{[1+r^{2}-2r(1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{4})]^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}$
$\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{[(1-r)^{2}+\frac{r}{2}\theta^{2}]^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}\leq 2\int_{0}^{\alpha}\Big[\frac{(1-r+\sqrt{\frac{r}{2}}\theta)^{2}}{2}\Big]^{-\frac{\varkappa}{2}}d\theta$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2^{1+\varkappa}}{r^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}\int_{0}^{\alpha}\Big[\theta+\frac{\sqrt{2}(1-r)}{\sqrt{r}}\Big]^{-\varkappa}d\theta\asymp\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
and
(6.17)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\geq\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{[1+r^{2}-2r(1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2})]^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}$
$\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{[(1-r)^{2}+r\theta^{2}]^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}\geq 2\int_{0}^{\alpha}[(1-r)+\sqrt{r}\theta]^{-\varkappa}d\theta$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{r^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}}\int_{0}^{\alpha}(\theta+\frac{1-r}{\sqrt{r}})^{-\varkappa}d\theta\asymp\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Combining (6.16) and (6.17), we get that, when  $\varkappa>1$ ,
(6.18)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}\asymp\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
for any  $\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ .
We now consider the case  $\alpha\in(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi]$ . On the one hand, we have
(6.19)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}>\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}.$
On the other hand, when  $\theta\in(\frac{\pi}{2},\alpha]\cup[-\alpha,-\frac{\pi}{2})$ , for any  $r\in(\frac{1}{2},1)$ , we have
$|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2}=1+r^{2}-2r\cos\theta\geq\frac{5}{4}.$
It follows that, when  $r\in(\frac{1}{2},1)$ ,
(6.20)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}+\int_{-\alpha}^{-\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}+(\frac{4}{5})^{\frac{\varkappa}{2}}(2\alpha-\pi).$
Consequently, we see from (6.19), (6.20), and (6.18) that (6.12) still hold for any  $\alpha\in(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi]$ .
This proves the lemma. ∎
Lemma 6.26.
Let  $\varkappa>0$ ,  $r\in(0,1)$ ,  $n\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $z_{j}=e^{i\arg z_{j}}$ ,  $j=1,2,\cdots,n$  be distinct points on  $\mathbb{T}$ . We assume that  $g$  is an analytic function in  $\Delta$  and satisfies that,
(1) there are two constants  $c_{0}>0$ ,  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that  $|g^{-1}(z)|\leq c_{0}$  for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ , and
(2) for each  $z_{j}$ ,  $j=1,2,\cdots,n$ , there are constants  $r_{j}\in(0,1)$ ,  $\vartheta_{j}>0$ ,  $C_{j}>0$  such that
$|g(z)|\leq C_{j}$  for all
$z\in\Omega_{j}:=\{z=re^{i\theta}:r_{j}<r<1,\arg z_{j}-\vartheta_{j}<\theta<\arg z_{j}+\vartheta_{j}\},$
and  $\Omega_{j_{1}}\cap\Omega_{j_{2}}=\emptyset$  whenever  $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ ,  $1\leq j_{1},j_{2}\leq n$ .
We define
$f(z)=g(z)\prod_{j=1}^{n}(z-z_{j}),z\in\Delta.$
Then, as  $r\rightarrow 1^{-}$ , we have
(6.21)
