$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|f(re^{i\theta})|^{\varkappa}}\asymp\begin{cases}\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\;\text{if}\;\varkappa>1,\\
\log\frac{1}{1-r},\;\;\;\text{if}\;\varkappa=1,\\
1,\quad\quad\quad\;\,\text{if}\;\varkappa\in(0,1).\end{cases}$
Proof.
We only prove (6.21) for the case when  $\varkappa>1$ . Other two cases can be proved by the similar way. For  $\varkappa>1$ . First we note that, for any  $0<r<1$ ,
(6.22)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|f(re^{i\theta})|^{\varkappa}}\geq\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{-{\alpha}_{j}+\arg z_{j}}^{\alpha_{j}+\arg z_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|f(re^{i\theta})|^{\varkappa}}.$
Meanwhile, in view of the conditions satisfied by  $g$ , we see that, for any  $1\leq j\leq n$ , it holds that  $|g(z)|\leq C^{*}$  for all  $z\in\widehat{\Omega}_{j}$ . Here  $C^{*}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq n}\{C_{j}\}$  and  $r^{*}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq n}\{r_{j}\}$ , and
$\widehat{\Omega}_{j}=\{z=re^{i\theta}:r^{*}<r<1,\arg z_{j}-\vartheta_{j}<\theta<\arg z_{j}+\vartheta_{j}\}.$
Hence, for each  $1\leq j\leq n$ , we have that, for any  $z=re^{i\theta}\in\widehat{\Omega}_{j}$ ,
(6.23)
$\displaystyle|f(z)|=|f(re^{i\theta})|$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{n}|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}||g(re^{i\theta})|$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle C^{*}\prod_{j=1}^{n}|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}|$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle 2^{n-1}C^{*}|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}|.$
Then it follows from (6.22), (6.23), and (6.12) that, when  $r>r^{*}$ ,
(6.24)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|f(re^{i\theta})|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle[2^{n-1}C^{*}]^{-\varkappa}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{-{\alpha}_{j}+\arg z_{j}}^{\alpha_{j}+\arg z_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle[2^{n-1}C^{*}]^{-\varkappa}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{-{\alpha}_{j}}^{\alpha_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle\asymp$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
On the other hand, we can write
$\prod_{j=1}^{n}(z-z_{j})^{-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{A_{j}}{z-z_{j}}.$
When  $r>r_{0}$ , we have
(6.25)
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|f(re^{i\theta})|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{A_{j}}{re^{i\theta}-z_{j}}\Big|^{\varkappa}\frac{d\theta}{|g(z)|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle{c_{0}}^{\varkappa}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{|A_{j}|}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}|}\Big]^{\varkappa}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle{c_{0}}^{\varkappa}n^{\varkappa-1}{\mathbb{A}}^{\varkappa}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg z_{j}}|^{\varkappa}}$
$\displaystyle\asymp$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\varkappa-1}},\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Here  ${\mathbb{A}}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq n}\{|A_{j}|\}$ . In (6.25), we have used the following inequality [31, Exercises 1.1.4, Page 11],
$\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}|a_{k}|\Big)^{p}\leq n^{p-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}|a_{k}|^{p},a_{k}\in\mathbb{C},p>1.$
Thus (6.21) for the case when  $\varkappa>1$  follows from (6.24) and (6.25). Finally, using the similar arguments above, and by (6.13), (6.14), we can obtain the remaining two cases of (6.21). The lemma is proved.
∎
We now present the proof of Theorem 6.20.
Proof of Theorem 6.20.
Let  $R\in({\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}})$ .
(A) It is easy to see that Theorem 6.20 holds for  $\tau=0$ .
(B) We now consider the case  $\tau<0$ .
$({\bf b_{1}})$  If  $R$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ . Then, we see that  $|R^{\prime}|^{\tau}$  is bounded above in a neighborhood of  $\mathbb{T}$ . Hence we obtain from the definition (6.11) of the generalized integral means spectrum that  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0$  for any  $\tau<0$ .
$({\bf b_{2}})$  We only prove the case for  $R\in\mathcal{Q}_{III}$ , other two cases can be proved similarly. If  $R\in\mathcal{Q}_{III}$  has at east one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Recall that, as in (6.10),  $R^{\prime}$  has the from as
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
We set
$g(z)=\frac{P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{\bf m}(z)},$
so that  $R^{\prime}(z)=g(z)\prod\limits_{n=1}^{s}(z-z_{n})$ . Then we see from the definition of  $R$  that
(1.1) there are two constants  $c_{0}>0$ ,  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that  $|g^{-1}(z)|\leq c_{0}$  for all  $|z|\in(r_{0},1)$ ,
and
(1.2) for each  $z_{n}=e^{i\arg z_{n}}$ ,  $n=1,2,\cdots,s$ , we can always find constants  $r_{n}\in(0,1)$ ,  $\vartheta_{n}>0$ ,  $C_{n}>0$  such that
$|g(z)|\leq C_{n}$  for all
$z\in\Omega_{n}=\{z=re^{i\theta}:r_{n}\leq r\leq 1,\arg z_{n}-\vartheta_{n}\leq\theta\leq\arg z_{n}+\vartheta_{n}\},$
and  $\Omega_{n_{1}}\cap\Omega_{n_{2}}=\emptyset$ , whenever  $n_{1}\neq n_{2}$ ,  $1\leq n_{1},n_{2}\leq s$ .
Then by using Lemma 6.26, we obtain that, as  $r\rightarrow 1^{-}$ ,
(6.26)
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{-\tau}}\asymp\begin{cases}\frac{1}{(1-r)^{-\tau-1}},\;\;\text{if}\;\tau<-1,\\
\log\frac{1}{1-r},\;\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\tau=-1,\\
1,\quad\quad\quad\;\,\;\;\text{if}\;\tau\in(-1,0).\end{cases}$
Note that for any small  $\epsilon>0$ ,
$\log\frac{1}{1-r}/\frac{1}{(1-r)^{\epsilon}}=(1-r)^{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{1-r}\rightarrow 0,\,\,{\text{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
This implies that  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(-1)=0$ . Then it follows from (6.26) that
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}0,\;\quad\,\,\,\;\,\text{for}\;\tau\in(-1,0),\\
|\tau|-1,\text{for}\;\tau\leq-1.\end{cases}$
(C) We next consider the case  $\tau>0$ .
$({\bf c_{1}})$  When  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{I}$ , we easily see that  ${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0$  for any  $\tau>0$ .
$({\bf c_{2}})$  When  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{II}$ . Recall that, as in (6.9),  $R^{\prime}$  has the form as
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{2}P_{{\bf m}}(z)}.$
We set
$Q_{1}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{{\bf m}}(z)}.$
Then, from the definition of  $R$ , we can find constants  $M>0$ ,  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ ,  $\eta_{j}\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2l})$ ,  $M_{j,1}>0,M_{j,2}>0$ ,  $j=1,2,\cdots,l$ , such that
$(\bf 2.1)$   $\Omega_{j_{1}}\cap\Omega_{j_{2}}=\emptyset$  whenever  $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ ,  $1\leq j_{1},j_{2}\leq l$ , and  $M_{j,2}\leq|Q_{1}(z)|\leq M_{j,1}$  for all  $z\in\Omega_{j}$ , here  $\Omega_{j}=\{re^{\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1,\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}\leq\theta\leq\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}\},$   $j=1,2,\cdots,l$ , and  $R$  has no critical points in  $\bigcup\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\Omega_{j}$ , and
$(\bf 2.2)$   $|R^{\prime}(z)|\leq M$  for all  $z\in\Omega_{0}-\bigcup\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\Omega_{j}$ , here  $\Omega_{0}=\{re^{\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1\}.$
For  $1\leq j\leq l$ , we take
$D^{j}:=\max\limits_{z\in\Omega_{j}}\{\prod\limits_{1\leq a\leq l,a\neq j}|z-e^{i\theta_{a}}|\},\,\,D_{j}:=\min\limits_{z\in\Omega_{j}}\{\prod\limits_{1\leq a\leq l,a\neq j}|z-e^{i\theta_{a}}|\}.$
In particular, when  $l=1$ , we take  $D^{1}=D_{1}=1$ . We define
$\mathbf{D}^{\ast}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\{D^{j}\},\,\,\,\mathbf{D}_{\ast}=\min\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\{D_{j}\}.$
It is easy to see that  $0<\mathbf{D}_{\ast}<\mathbf{D}^{\ast}<+\infty$  since  $\Omega_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,l$  are all compact. Then, when  $r>r_{0}$ , we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}\frac{|Q_{1}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{j}}|^{2\tau}}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq$
$\displaystyle M_{2}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}^{*}]^{-2\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{j}}|^{2\tau}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle M_{2}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}^{*}]^{-2\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}},$
here  $M_{2}=\min\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\{M_{j,2}\}$ , and
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta+2\pi M^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle M_{1}^{\tau}[{\bf{D}}_{*}]^{-2\tau}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{j}}|^{2\tau}}+2\pi M^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle M_{1}^{\tau}[{\bf{D}}_{*}]^{-2\tau}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}}+2\pi M^{\tau},$
here,  $M_{1}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}\{M_{j,1}\}$ .
Consequently, from Lemma 6.24, when  $r>r_{0}$ , we obtain that, for  $\tau>\frac{1}{2}$ ,
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta\asymp\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}}\asymp\frac{1}{(1-r)^{2\tau-1}},\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
and for  $\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{2}]$ ,  $\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta\asymp\begin{cases}\log\frac{1}{1-r},\;\;\text{if}\;\tau=\frac{1}{2},\\
1,\quad\quad\quad\,\text{if}\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{2}).\end{cases}$
It follows that
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}2\tau-1,\,\text{for}\;\tau>\frac{1}{2},\\
0,\quad\,\,\;\;\;\;\text{for}\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{2}].\end{cases}$
$({\bf c_{3}})$  When  $R$  belongs to the class  $\mathcal{Q}_{III}$ . The main idea of the proof of this case is similar to the case  $({\bf c_{2}})$ . Recall that, as in (6.10),
(6.27)
$\displaystyle R^{\prime}(z)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{\prod\limits_{j=1}^{l}(z-e^{i\theta_{j}})^{3}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{t}(z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}})^{2}P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
We let
$Q_{2}(z)=\frac{[(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots(z-z_{s})]P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Then, when  $t\in\mathbb{N}$ , we see from the definition of  $R$  that there are constants  $M>0$ ,  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ , and  $\eta_{j}\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2(l+t)})$ ,  $M_{j,1}>0,M_{j,2}>0$ ,  $j=1,2,\cdots,l$ , and  $\widetilde{\eta}_{k}\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2(l+t)})$ ,  $\widetilde{M}_{k,1}>0,\widetilde{M}_{k,2}>0$ ,  $k=1,2,\cdots t$ , such that
$(\bf 3.1)$   $\Omega_{j_{1}}\cap\Omega_{j_{2}}=\emptyset$  whenever  $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$  and  $M_{j,2}\leq|Q_{2}(z)|\leq M_{j,1}$  for all  $z\in\Omega_{j}$ , here  $\Omega_{j}=\{re^{\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1,\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}\leq\theta\leq\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}\},$   $1\leq j_{1},j_{2}\leq l,$  and
$(\bf 3.2)$   $\widetilde{\Omega}_{k_{1}}\cap\widetilde{\Omega}_{k_{2}}=\emptyset$  whenever  $k_{1}\neq k_{2}$ ,  $1\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq t$ , and  ${\Omega}_{j}\cap\widetilde{\Omega}_{k}=\emptyset$  for all  $1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t$ , and  $\widetilde{M}_{k,2}\leq|Q_{2}(z)|\leq\widetilde{M}_{k,1}$  for all  $z\in\widetilde{\Omega}_{k}$ , here  $\widetilde{\Omega}_{k}=\{re^{\theta}:{r}_{0}\leq r\leq 1,\widetilde{\theta}_{k}-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}\leq\theta\leq\widetilde{\theta}_{k}+\widetilde{\eta}_{k}\},$  and  $R$  has no critical points in  $\bigcup\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}(\Omega_{j}\bigcup\widetilde{\Omega}_{k})$ , and
$(\bf 3.3)$   $|R^{\prime}(z)|\leq M$  for all  $z\in\Omega_{0}-\bigcup\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}(\Omega_{j}\bigcup\widetilde{\Omega}_{k})$ , here
$\Omega_{0}=\{re^{\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1\}.$
For  $1\leq j\leq l$ , we let  $\widetilde{\pi}(z):=\prod\limits_{1\leq k\leq t}|z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}}|^{2}\}$  and take
$\mathcal{D}^{j}:=\max\limits_{z\in\Omega_{j}}\{\widetilde{\pi}(z)\prod\limits_{1\leq a\leq l,a\neq j}|z-e^{i\theta_{a}}|^{3}\},\,\,\mathcal{D}_{j}:=\min\limits_{z\in\Omega_{j}}\{\widetilde{\pi}(z)\prod\limits_{1\leq a\leq l,a\neq j}|z-e^{i\theta_{a}}|^{3}\}.$
In particular, when  $l=1$ , we take  $\mathcal{D}^{1}=\max\limits_{z\in\Omega_{1}}\widetilde{\pi}(z),\,\,\mathcal{D}_{1}=\min\limits_{z\in\Omega_{1}}\widetilde{\pi}(z).$
For  $1\leq k\leq t$ , we let  $\pi(z):=\prod\limits_{1\leq j\leq l}|z-e^{i{\theta}_{j}}|^{3}$  and take
$\widetilde{D}^{k}:=\max\limits_{z\in\widetilde{\Omega}_{k}}\{\pi(z)\prod\limits_{1\leq b\leq t,b\neq k}|z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{b}}|^{2}\},\,\,\widetilde{D}_{k}:=\min\limits_{z\in\widetilde{\Omega}_{k}}\{\pi(z)\prod\limits_{1\leq b\leq t,b\neq k}|z-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{b}}|^{2}\}.$
In particular, when  $t=1$ , we take  $\widetilde{D}^{1}=\max\limits_{z\in\widetilde{\Omega}_{1}}\pi(z),\,\,\widetilde{D}_{1}=\min\limits_{z\in\widetilde{\Omega}_{1}}\pi(z).$
We define
$\mathbf{D}^{\star}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}\{\mathcal{D}^{j},\widetilde{D}^{k}\},\,\,\mathbf{D}_{\star}=\min\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}\{\mathcal{D}_{j},\widetilde{D}_{k}\}.$
We easily see that  $0<\mathbf{D}_{\star}<\mathbf{D}^{\star}<+\infty$  from the compactness of  $\Omega_{j},j=1,2,\cdots,l$ , and  $\widetilde{\Omega}_{k},k=1,2,\cdots,t$ . Then, when  $r>r_{0}$ , we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta\geq\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\int_{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}+\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\geq M_{2}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}^{\star}]^{-\tau}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{j}}|^{3\tau}}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\int_{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}+\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}}|^{2\tau}}\Big]$
$\displaystyle=M_{2}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}^{\star}]^{-\tau}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{3\tau}}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\int_{-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}}\Big],$
here  $M_{2}=\min\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}\{M_{j,2},\widetilde{M}_{k,2}\}$ , and
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta\leq\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta+\sum\limits_{k=1}^{t}\int_{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}+\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta+2\pi M^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle\leq M_{1}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}_{\star}]^{-\tau}\Big[\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int_{\theta_{j}-\eta_{j}}^{\theta_{j}+\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{j}}|^{3\tau}}+\sum\limits_{k=1}^{t}\int_{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\theta}_{k}+\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\widetilde{\theta}_{k}}|^{2\tau}}\Big]+2\pi M^{\tau}$
$\displaystyle=M_{1}^{\tau}[\mathbf{D}_{\star}]^{-\tau}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{3\tau}}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\int_{-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}}\Big]+2\pi M^{\tau},$
here,  $M_{1}=\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq l,1\leq k\leq t}\{M_{j,1},\widetilde{M}_{k,1}\}$ .
Consequently, from Lemma 6.24, when  $r>r_{0}$ , we obtain that, for  $\tau>\frac{1}{3}$ ,
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta$
$\displaystyle\asymp$
$\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int_{-\eta_{j}}^{\eta_{j}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{3\tau}}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\int_{-\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}^{\widetilde{\eta}_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\tau}}$
$\displaystyle\asymp$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{(1-r)^{3\tau-1}},\,\,\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
and for  $\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{3}]$ ,  $\text{as}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|R^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{\tau}d\theta\asymp\begin{cases}\log\frac{1}{1-r},\;\;\text{if}\;\tau=\frac{1}{3},\\
1,\quad\quad\quad\text{if}\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{3}).\end{cases}$
It follows that
(6.28)
${\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}3\tau-1,\,\text{for}\;\tau>\frac{1}{3},\\
0,\quad\,\,\;\;\;\;\text{for}\;\tau\in(0,\frac{1}{3}].\end{cases}$
For the remaining case when  $t=0$ , by the similar way as in the case  $({\bf c_{2}})$ , we still can prove that (6.28) holds. Finally, combining all above arguments, we conclude that Theorem 6.20 is true. This finishes‌ the proof of Theorem 6.20.
∎
Remark 6.27.
We recall the Schwarz-Christoffel formula for the unit disk, see [1, Page 236]. Let  $f$  be a univalent function (conformal map) from the unit disk  $\Delta$  onto the interior of a bounded polygon  $\mathcal{P}$  with vertices  $z_{1},\dots,z_{n},n\geq 3$ , and corresponding interior angles  $\alpha_{1}\pi,\dots,\alpha_{n}\pi$ . Then the derivative of  $f$  is given by
$f^{\prime}(z)=C\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(z-{a_{k}}\right)^{\alpha_{k}-1},\quad z\in\Delta,$
where  $a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}$  are points on the unit circle  $\mathbb{T}$  and  $C$  is a non-zero complex constant.
Note that for  $r\in(0,1)$ ,
$\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{|f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})|^{2}}=|C|^{-2}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta}{\prod\limits_{k=1}^{n}\left|re^{i\theta}-{e^{i\arg a_{k}}}\right|^{2\alpha_{k}-2}}.$
Since  $\alpha_{k}<2$  for each  $k$ , a direct estimate using Lemma 6.24 and similar arguments in the proof of part  $(\bf c_{3})$  of Theorem 6.20 shows that  $\beta_{f}(-2)<1$ . Actually, let
${\bf{\pi}}(z)={\bf{\pi}}(re^{i\theta})=\frac{1}{\prod\limits_{k=1}^{n}\left|re^{i\theta}-{e^{i\arg a_{k}}}\right|^{2\alpha_{k}-2}}.$
For a given  $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ , we can find constants  $M>0$ ,  $\eta_{k}\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2n})$ ,  $k=1,2,\cdots,n$  such that  $\Omega_{k_{1}}\cap\Omega_{k_{2}}=\emptyset$  whenever  $k_{1}\neq k_{2}$ ,  $1\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq n,$  here  $\Omega_{k}=\{re^{\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1,\arg a_{k}-\eta_{k}\leq\theta\leq\arg a_{k}+\eta_{k}\},$  and  $|{\bf{\pi}}(z)|\leq M$  for all  $z\in\Omega-\bigcup\limits_{1\leq k\leq n}\Omega_{k}$ , here  $\Omega=\{re^{i\theta}:r_{0}\leq r\leq 1\}$ .
For  $1\leq k\leq n$ , we take
$D^{k}:=\max\limits_{z\in\Omega_{k}}\{\prod\limits_{1\leq b\leq n,b\neq k}|z-e^{i\arg a_{k}}|^{2-2\alpha_{k}}\}.$
We define  ${\bf\mathfrak{D}}^{\ast}=\max\limits_{1\leq k\leq n}\{D_{k}\}.$  Then we easily see that  $0<\mathfrak{D}^{\ast}<+\infty$  since  $\Omega_{k},k=1,2,\cdots,n$  are all compact. Hence, when  $r>r_{0}$ , we have
$\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\pi(re^{i\theta})d\theta$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\int_{\arg a_{k}-\eta_{k}}^{\arg a_{k}+\eta_{k}}\pi(re^{i\theta})d\theta+2\pi M$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle[\mathfrak{D}^{\ast}]^{2}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\int_{\arg a_{k}-\eta_{k}}^{\arg a_{k}+\eta_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|re^{i\theta}-e^{i\arg a_{k}}|^{2\alpha_{k}-2}}+2\pi M$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle[\mathfrak{D}^{\ast}]^{2}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\int_{-\eta_{k}}^{\eta_{k}}\frac{d\theta}{|1-re^{i\theta}|^{2\alpha_{k}-2}}+2\pi M.$
Consequently, from Lemma 6.24 and the fact that  $\alpha_{k}<2$  for every  $k$ , we conclude that  $\beta_{f}(-2)<1$ . That is to say, the Brennan conjecture holds for all univalent functions from  $\Delta$  onto the interior of a bounded polygon  $\mathcal{P}$ .
7. Remarks
7.1. The first part of remarks
We know that
Proposition 7.1 ([39], Proposition 3.2, 3.3).
The mapping  $\Lambda_{1}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto N_{f_{\mu}}$  from  $(T,d_{T})$  to its image  $T_{1}$  in  $E_{1}$  is a homeomorphism, and the mapping  $\Lambda_{2}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto S_{f_{\mu}}$  from  $(T,d_{T})$  to its image  $T_{2}$  in  $E_{2}$  is a homeomorphism.
Remark 7.2.
In view of Propposition 7.1, we can identify the universal Teichmüller space with  $T_{1}$  or  $T_{2}$ .
We let  $\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}$  be the class of all functions  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$  with  $f(\infty)=\infty$ . We set
$\mathbf{N}_{q}:=\{\phi:\phi=N_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}\},\,\,\,\mathbf{S}_{q}:=\{\phi:\phi=S_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}\}.$
It is easy to see that  $T_{1}=\mathbf{N}_{q}$  and  $T_{2}=\mathbf{S}_{q}$ . We now identify the closure of universal Teichmüller space with  $\overline{T}_{1}=\overline{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$  in  $\mathbf{N}$  or  $\overline{T}_{2}=\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{q}$  in  $\bf{S}$ . On the other hand, we know that  $\overline{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$  is contained in  $\overline{\mathcal{T}}$ , and for any  $\phi\in{\mathbf{S}}_{q}$ , we can take a unique univalent function  $f_{\phi}(z)\in\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}$  with  $\phi(z)=S_{f_{\phi}}(z)$ . Hence, the IMS functional  $I_{{T}_{2}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau),\phi\in{{\mathbf{S}}}_{q}$  is well-defined. It follows from Theorem 1.12 and 1.14 and Proposition 7.1 that
Corollary 7.3.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{\overline{T}_{1}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)$  is continuous on  $\overline{{T}}_{1}=\overline{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ .
Corollary 7.4.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ , the IMS functional  $I_{T_{2}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)$  is continuous on  $T_{2}={\mathbf{S}}_{q}$ .
Remark 7.5.
We let  $\mathcal{S}_{Q}$  be the class of all univalent functions  $f$  which belong to  $\mathcal{S}$  and admit a quasiconformal extension to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ . It is easy to see that  $\mathcal{S}_{q}$  is a proper subset of  $\mathcal{S}_{Q}$ .
For each  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ , let  $\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$  be the subclass of  $\mathcal{S}_{Q}$  which consists of all the functions  $f$  satisfying that  $\lim\limits_{\Delta\ni z\rightarrow e^{i\theta}}f(z)=\infty$ . For each  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ ,  $\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$  is a copy of the universal Teichmüller space.
By using [58, Lemma 1] and repeating the arguments in the proof of Theorem 1.15, we can similarly prove that
Proposition 7.6.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ . For each  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ , we have  $\beta_{f}(\tau)<B(\tau)$  for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$ .
Remark 7.7.
For  $f,g\in\mathcal{S}$ , by checking the proof of Proposition 4.7, we see that  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=\beta_{g}(\tau)$  for each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$  if  $N_{f}-N_{g}\in E_{1,0}$ . Then, combining Theorem 1.15, Proposition 7.6, we obtain that, if  $f$  satisfies that  $N_{f}$  is equivalent to some  $N_{f_{q}}$  in  $E_{1}$ , here  $f_{q}\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}$ , then  $\beta_{f}(\tau)<B(\tau)$  for any  $\tau\neq 0$  so that  $f$  can not be an extremal function for any  $B(\tau)$  with  $\tau\neq 0$ .
We let
$\mathbf{S}_{\theta}:=\{\phi,\phi=S_{f}(z),\,f\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}\}.$
If  $\phi\in\mathbf{S}_{\theta}$ , then there is a unique univalent function  $f_{\phi}$  with  $f_{\phi}\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$  and such that  $\phi(z)=S_{f_{\phi}}(z).$  If  $\phi\in\partial\mathbf{S}_{\theta}$ , we know that there is a sequence  $\{f_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ ,  $f_{n}\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$ , such that  $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|S_{f_{n}}-\phi\|_{E_{2}}=0,$  and the sequence  $\{f_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$  converges for every  $z\in\Delta$ . Then, taking  $f_{\phi}(z)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}f_{n}(z),z\in\Delta$ , we see that  $f_{\phi}\in\mathcal{S}$  with  $\phi(z)=S_{f_{\phi}}(z),$  and  $f_{\phi}$  is unique by the normalization. Here the statement  $f_{\phi}$  is unique means that, if there is another sequence  $\{\widehat{f}_{n}(z)\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ ,  $\widehat{f}_{n}\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}$ , such that  $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|S_{\widehat{f}_{n}}-\phi\|_{E_{2}}=0,$  and the sequence  $\{\widehat{f}_{n}(z)\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$  converges for every  $z\in\Delta$ , then, take  $\widehat{f}_{\phi}(z)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\widehat{f}_{n}(z)$ , we have  $\widehat{f}_{\phi}(z)=f_{\phi}(z)$  for all  $z\in\Delta$ . From these, for any  $\phi\in\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{\theta}$ , we can take a unique univalent function  $f_{\phi}(z)$  with  $f_{\phi}\in\mathcal{S}$  and such that  $\phi(z)=S_{f_{\phi}}(z).$  Thus, the IMS functional  $I_{\overline{T}_{\theta}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau),\phi\in\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{\theta}$  is well-defined. From [6], we know that the boundary  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{\theta}$  of  $\mathbf{S}_{\theta}$  is larger than the one of  $\mathbf{N}_{q}$ . It is interesting to study
Problem 7.8.
For each  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ , is the IMS functional  $I_{\overline{T}_{\theta}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau)$  continuous on  $\overline{T}_{2}=\overline{{\mathbf{S}}}_{\theta}$  when  $\tau\neq 0$ ?
Remark 7.9.
Let  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ . We know from [39] that  $\mathcal{E}_{1}(z)=-\log(1-z)$  is an extremal function for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  when  $\tau\geq 2$ , and  $\mathcal{E}_{2}(z)=z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2}$  is an extremal function for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  when  $\tau\leq\tau_{*}$ . Here  $\tau_{*}$  is the same as in Theorem 1.3. Also, both  $N_{\mathcal{E}_{1}}(z)$  and  $N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}$  lie on the boundary of  $\mathcal{T}$ . In view of these facts and Theorem 1.15, we will say an extremal function for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  is regular if its Pre-Schwarzian derivative lies on the boundary of  $\mathcal{T}$ . We then raise the following general
Conjecture 7.10.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ ,  $B_{b}(\tau)$  has at least one regular extremal function.
If Conjecture 7.10 is true, then the following conjecture will follow.
Conjecture 7.11.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ ,  $B_{b}(\tau)$  has at least one extremal function whose Schwarzian derivative lies on the boundary  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}$  of  $\mathbf{S}_{Q}$ .
Here,  ${\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$  is defined as
(7.1)
${\mathbf{S}}_{Q}:=\{\phi:\phi=S_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}\}.$
We easily see that  ${\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$  coincides with  $\mathbf{S}_{q}$  by using (2.2).
7.2. The second part of remarks
When  $\tau\leq-2$ , we find that there are some univalent functions  $f$  satisfying that  $\beta_{f}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  and  $\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=6$ . For instance,
$\kappa(z)=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{2}},\,\,\mathcal{E}_{2}(z)=P_{2}(z)=z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2},\,\,P_{3}(z)=z-\frac{1}{3}z^{3},z\in\Delta,$
which have been mentioned before. We have known that  $\beta_{\kappa}(\tau)=\beta_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(\tau)=\beta_{P_{3}}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  for  $\tau\leq-2$ . On the other hand, by a simply computation, we obtain that
$S_{\kappa}(z)=-\frac{6}{(1-z^{2})^{2}},\,S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(z)=-\frac{3}{2}\frac{1}{(1-z)^{2}},\,S_{P_{3}}(z)=\frac{-2-4z^{2}}{(1-z^{2})^{2}},\,z\in\Delta.$
It follows that  $\|S_{\kappa}\|_{E_{2}}=\|S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}\|_{E_{2}}=\|S_{P_{3}}\|_{E_{2}}=6$ . We will provide more functions that have these characteristics.
Example 7.12.
We consider the  $T$ -symmetric Koebe functions  $\kappa_{T}$ , see [19], which are defined as
$\kappa_{T}(z):=\frac{z}{(1-z^{T})^{\frac{2}{T}}},z\in\Delta,T\in\mathbb{N}.$
We see that  $\kappa_{1}(z)=\kappa(z)$  and
(7.2)
$\kappa^{\prime}_{T}(z)=\frac{(1+z^{T})}{(1-z^{T})^{1+\frac{2}{T}}},z\in\Delta,$
$S_{\kappa_{T}}(z)=\frac{2(T^{2}-1)z^{3T-2}-2(T^{2}+2)z^{2T-2}+2(T^{2}-1)z^{T-2}}{(1-z^{2T})^{2}},z\in\Delta.$
In particular,
$S_{\kappa_{2}}(z)=\frac{6}{(1+z^{2})^{2}}.$
In view of Lemma 6.26, we obtain from (7.2) that  $\beta_{\kappa_{T}}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  for each  $T\in\mathbb{N}$  when  $\tau\leq-2$ . Also, it is not hard to check that, for each  $T\in\mathbb{N}$ ,
$(1-|z|^{2})^{2}|S_{\kappa_{T}}(z)|\rightarrow 6,\,\,{\text{as}}\,\,z\rightarrow e^{\frac{k\pi}{T}i}\,\text{radially}.$
Here  $k=1,3,\cdots,2T-1$ . Hence  $\|S_{\kappa_{T}}\|_{E_{2}}=6$  for each  $T\in\mathbb{N}$ .
Example 7.13.
Now, we consider the so-called  $\gamma$ -spiral Koebe functions  $f_{\gamma}$ , which are defined as
$f_{\gamma}(z):={z}(1-z)^{-2e^{i\gamma}cos\gamma},z\in\Delta,$
for  $\gamma\in(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ , see [46]. We see that  $f_{0}$  is the Koebe function. A direct computation yields that
$f^{\prime}_{\gamma}(z)=\frac{1+ze^{2i\gamma}}{(1-z)^{1+2e^{i\gamma}cos\gamma}},z\in\Delta.$
It follows from Lemma 6.26 again that  $\beta_{f_{\gamma}}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  for each  $\gamma\in(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$  when  $\tau\leq-2$ , and it has been proved in [46] that  $\|S_{f_{\gamma}}\|_{E_{2}}=6$ .
Moreover, we observe that
Proposition 7.14.
Let  $\tau\leq-2$ ,  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . If  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then  $\beta_{R}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  and  $\|S_{R}\|_{E_{2}}=6.$
Proof.
Note that  $\beta_{R}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  follows from Theorem 6.20. We only need to prove  $\|S_{R}\|_{E_{2}}=6.$  If  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , we write
$R^{\prime}(z)=\frac{(z-e^{i\theta})P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)},$
here  $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ , the polynomials  $(z-e^{i\theta})P_{\bf n}$  and  $P_{\bf m}$  have no common factors except  $1$ , and  $P_{\bf n}(e^{i\theta})\neq 0$ . We let
$\varphi(z)=\frac{P_{\bf n}(z)}{P_{\bf m}(z)}.$
Then  $\varphi$  is analytic in  $\Delta$ , and is analytic at the point  $e^{i\theta}$  with  $\varphi(e^{i\theta})\neq 0$ . Consequently, from
$R^{\prime\prime}(z)=\varphi(z)+(z-e^{i\theta})\varphi^{\prime}(z),$
and
$R^{\prime\prime\prime}(z)=2\varphi^{\prime}(z)+(z-e^{i\theta})\varphi^{\prime\prime}(z),$
we obtain that
$\displaystyle|S_{R}(z)|$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\Big|\frac{R^{\prime\prime\prime}(z)}{R^{\prime}(z)}-\frac{3}{2}\Big[\frac{R^{\prime\prime}(z)}{R^{\prime}(z)}\Big]^{2}\Big|$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{|[\varphi^{\prime}(z)+(z-e^{i\theta})\varphi^{\prime\prime}(z)](z-e^{i\theta})\varphi(z)-\frac{3}{2}[\varphi(z)+(z-e^{i\theta})\varphi^{\prime}(z)]^{2}|}{|1-ze^{-i\theta}|^{2}|\varphi(z)|^{2}}.$
Hence, we see that  $|S_{R}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{2}\rightarrow 6$ , as  $z\rightarrow e^{i\theta}$  radially. The proposition is proved.
∎
Meanwhile, if Conjecture 1.4 is true, then  $\kappa_{T}$ ,  $f_{\gamma}$  and any  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  that have at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , are all the extremal functions for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  when  $\tau\leq-2$ . From these, it is reasonable to guess that
Conjecture 7.15.
When  $\tau\leq-2$ , the extremal function  $f$  for  $B_{b}(\tau)$  should satisfy that  $\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=6$ .
7.3. The third part of remarks
Remark 7.16.
Let  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{P}$ . If  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then, from Theorem 1.15, Proposition 7.6, Theorem 1.3, and the fact that  $\beta_{R}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  for  $\tau\leq-2$ , we know that  $R$  does not belong to  $\mathcal{S}_{Q}$  (defined as in Remark 7.5), and the Schwarzian derivative  $S_{R}$  of  $R$  may lie on  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}$  (here  $\mathbf{S}_{Q}$  is defined as in (7.1)).
For example, the function  $\mathcal{E}_{2}(z)=z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2}$  has a critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , and we know from [39, Remark 5.9] that  $S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}$  lies on  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}$ . Hence we believe that  $S_{R}$  should lie on the boundary of  $\mathbf{S}_{Q}$  if  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , although we have not found a proof for this claim. We leave it as the following
Conjecture 7.17.
Let  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . Then  $S_{R}$  lies on  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}$  if  $R$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
We define the closed subspace  $E_{1,0}$  of  $E_{1}$  as
$E_{1,0}:=\{\phi\in E_{1}:\lim\limits_{|z|\rightarrow 1^{-}}\phi(z)(1-|z|^{2})=0\}.$
We say two elements  $\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\in E_{1}$  are equivalent, if  $\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}\in E_{1,0}$ . The equivalence class of  $\phi\in E_{1}$  is denoted by  $[\phi]_{E_{1}}$ . The set of all equivalence classes  $[\phi]_{E_{1}}$  will be denote by  $E_{1}/E_{1,0}$ .  $E_{1}/E_{1,0}$  is a Banach space with the quotient norm
$\|[\phi]_{E_{1}}\|:=\inf\limits_{\psi\in[\phi]_{E_{1}}}\|\psi\|_{E_{1}}=\inf\limits_{\psi\in E_{1,0}}\|\phi+\psi\|_{E_{1}}.$
We let  $\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}:[\mu]_{AT}\mapsto[N_{f_{\mu}}]_{E_{1}}.$
The mapping  $\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}$  is called asymptotic Pre-Bers map. It has been proved in [39] that
Proposition 7.18.
The mapping  $\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}$  from  $(AT,d_{AT})$  to  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$  in  $E_{1}/E_{1,0}$  is a homeomorphism.
Here,  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}:=\{[\phi]_{E_{1}}:\phi=N_{f}(z),\,f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}\}$  is an open subset of  $E_{1}/E_{1,0}$ .
Remark 7.19.
In view of Proposition 7.18, we can identify the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space  $AT$  with  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ .
Remark 7.20.
Let  $P_{n}\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$ . If  $P_{n}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then it is easy to check that  $N_{P_{n}}$  is contained in  $E_{1,0}$  so that  $N_{P_{n}}$  belongs to the class  $[0]_{E_{1}}$  in  $E_{1}/E_{1,0}$ . On the other hand, if  $P_{n}$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , then we see that there is no function  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$  such that  $N_{P_{n}}-N_{f}\in E_{1,0}$ . Actually, if there is a function  $f_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$  such that  $N_{P_{n}}-N_{f_{0}}\in E_{1,0}$ , then, by using the same arguments as in the proof of Proposition 4.7, we obtain that  $\beta_{f_{0}}(\tau)=\beta_{P_{n}}(\tau)=|\tau|-1$  for  $\tau\leq-2$ , which contradicts Theorem 1.3 and 1.15. Hence, we further raise the following dichotomy conjecture for univalent polynomials.
Conjecture 7.21.
Let  $P_{n}\in{\mathcal{U}}_{P}$ . Then (1)  $[N_{P_{n}}]_{E_{1}}$  lies on the origin, i.e.,  $[0]_{E_{1}}$ , of the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ , if  $P_{n}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ ; (2)
$[N_{P_{n}}]_{E_{1}}$  lies on the boundary of  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ , if  $P_{n}$  has at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Remark 7.22.
As remarked above, the proof of part (1) of Conjecture 7.21 is easy. However, checking the validity of part (2) of Conjecture 7.21 seems not easy. We will give an example for part (2) of Conjecture 7.21. We consider again the function  $\mathcal{E}_{2}(z)=z-\frac{1}{2}z^{2}$  which has one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$  and belongs to  $\partial\mathcal{T}$ .
It is known from [39, Remark 5.9  $({\bf II})$ ] that
(7.3)
$\lim\limits_{\gamma\rightarrow 1^{-}}\|N_{g_{\gamma}}-N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}\|_{E_{1}}=0.$
Here,  $g_{\gamma}(z):=[(1-z)^{1+\gamma}-1]/(-\gamma-1),\gamma\in(0,1)$  are univalent functions in  $\Delta$  which admit a quasiconformal extension to  $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ . Consequently, note that  $g_{\gamma},\gamma\in(0,1)$  are all bounded in  $\Delta$ , we can find a family of functions  $f_{\gamma}\in\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\infty}$  such that  $\varsigma_{\gamma}\circ f_{\gamma}=g_{\gamma},z\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$  so that  $N_{f_{\gamma}}-N_{g_{\gamma}}\in E_{1,0}$  for each  $\gamma\in(0,1)$ . Here  $\varsigma_{\gamma}$  are the Möbius transformations with the form  $\varsigma_{\gamma}(\eta)=\frac{\eta}{1+\eta a_{\gamma}}$ ,  $a_{\gamma}\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}},a_{\gamma}^{-1}\neq\overline{g_{\gamma}(\Delta)}$ . Then, from the fact
$\|[N_{g_{\gamma}}]_{E_{1}}-[N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}]_{E_{1}}\|\leq\|N_{g_{\gamma}}-N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}\|_{E_{1}},$
and (7.3), we obtain that
$\lim\limits_{\gamma\rightarrow 1^{-}}\|[N_{f_{\gamma}}]_{E_{1}}-[N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}]_{E_{1}}\|=\lim\limits_{\gamma\rightarrow 1^{-}}\|[N_{g_{\gamma}}]_{E_{1}}-[N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}]_{E_{1}}\|=0.$
On the other hand, from Remark 7.19, we know that there is no functions  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$  such that  $N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}-N_{f}\in E_{1,0}.$  Combining these facts, we have checked that  $[N_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}]_{E_{1}}$  lies on the boundary of  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ .
Remark 7.23.
When  $P_{n}\in\mathcal{U}_{P}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ , we have pointed out that  $N_{P_{n}}$  belongs to  ${E_{1,0}}$ . On the other hand, for a univalent function (conformal mapping)  $f$  from  $\Delta$  to a bounded Jordan domain in  $\mathbb{C}$ , we know that  $f$  is an asymptotically conformal mapping if and only if  $N_{f}$  belongs to  $E_{1,0}$ , see [26], [48] or [50]. Hence it is natural to ask whether  $P_{n}$  is an asymptotically conformal mapping in  $\Delta$  when  $P_{n}\in\mathcal{U}_{P}$  has no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$ . However, we find that there exists  $P_{n}\in\mathcal{U}_{P}$  with no critical points on  $\mathbb{T}$  for which  $P_{n}(\mathbb{T})$  is not a bounded Jordan curve so that  $P_{n}$  cannot be asymptotically conformal. As an example, we consider  ${\bf{P}}(z):=z+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}z^{2}+\frac{1}{4}z^{3},z\in\Delta.$  Note that  ${\bf{P}}(z)=\pi_{2}\circ\overline{{\bf{P}}}\circ\pi_{1}(z),z\in\Delta$ . Here,  $w=\pi_{1}(z)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}z$ , which maps  $\Delta$  conformally to the disk  $\Delta(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\{w\in\mathbb{C}:|w|<\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\}$ ,  $\zeta=\overline{{\bf{P}}}(w)=(1+w)^{3}-1$ ,  $\pi_{2}(\zeta)=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\zeta$ . Then, by Corollary 5.7.3 in [53, Page 197], we obtain that  ${\bf{P}}$  belongs to  $\mathcal{U}_{P}$ , or we can check this fact by using Dieudonné’s univalence criterion, see [20, Page 75]. Meanwhile, we see from  ${\bf{P}}^{\prime}(z)=(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}z+1)^{2}$  that  ${\bf{P}}^{\prime}\neq 0$  for any  $|z|<2/\sqrt{3}$ . Also, we easily check that  ${\bf{P}}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}i)={\bf{P}}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}i)$ , which means that the curve  ${\bf P}(\mathbb{T})$  is not a bounded Jordan curve in  $\mathbb{C}$ .
Remark 7.24.
If Conjecture 7.10 holds, namely,  $B_{b}(\tau)$  has an extremal function  $f$  whose Pre-Schwarzian derivative lies on  $\partial\mathcal{T}$ , then, by using the same arguments as in Remark 7.22, we can obtain that  $[N_{f}]_{E_{1}}$  lies on the boundary of  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ . This means that Conjecture 7.10 implies that
Conjecture 7.25.
For each  $\tau\in\mathbb{C}$ ,  $B_{b}(\tau)$  has at least one extremal function  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  such that  $[N_{f}]_{E_{1}}$  lies on the boundary of the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space  $\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}$ .
7.4. The final part of remarks
In the paper [54], Shimorin introduced and studied the following multiplication operator  $\mathcal{M}_{f}$ , induced by the Schwarzian derivative of univalent function  $f\in\mathcal{S}$ ,
$\mathcal{M}_{f}(\phi)(z):=S_{f}(z)\phi(z),\,\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta).$
There is a close connection between the norm of multiplication operator  $\mathcal{M}_{f}$  and the Brennan conjecture. It has been proved in [54] that
Proposition 7.26.
If some univalent function  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  satisfies that
(7.4)
$\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|^{2}\leq\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)},$
for any  $\alpha>0$ . Then  $\beta_{f}(-2)\leq 1$ , that is to say, the Brennan conjecture is true for the function  $f$ .
Here,
$\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}\neq 0,\phi\in\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)}\frac{\|S_{f}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}}{\|\phi(z)\|_{\alpha}}:=\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).$
Remark 7.27.
It is easy to see that, if for any  $\alpha>0$ , (7.4) holds for all  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}$ , then the Brennan conjecture is true. On the other hand, it has been pointed out in [54, Page 1633] that there exists univalent function  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  such that
$\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  when  $\alpha>-1$ . Meanwhile, for any  $\alpha>-1$ , it has been shown in [54] that,
(7.5)
$\mathbb{M}_{\kappa_{\Theta}}^{2}(\alpha)=\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.$
Here,  $\kappa_{\Theta}$  are the Koebe function  $\kappa$  and its rotations, which are defined as
(7.6)
$\kappa_{\Theta}(z):=\frac{z}{(1-e^{i\Theta}z)^{2}},\,\Theta\in(-\pi,\pi],\,z\in\Delta.$
Let  $\varrho$  be a Möbius transformation. We conclude that  $\varrho\circ\kappa_{\Theta}\in\mathcal{S}$ , if and only if  $\varrho$  has the form as
$\varrho(\zeta):=\varrho_{c}(\zeta)=\frac{\zeta}{1+ce^{i\Theta}\zeta},0\leq c\leq 4.$
Since the Schwarzian derivative is invariant under the Möbius transformation, we see that, for any  $\alpha>-1$ , it holds that  $\mathbb{M}_{\varrho_{c}\circ\kappa_{\Theta}}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha),$  for any  $(c,\Theta)\in[0,4]\times(-\pi,\pi]$ . Because the Koebe function and its rotations are the unique class of extremal functions in  $\mathcal{S}$  for some extremal problems in the theory of univalent functions, thus, it is natural to guess that the functions  $\varrho_{c}\circ\kappa_{\Theta}$ ,  $(c,\Theta)\in[0,4]\times(-\pi,\pi]$ , may be the unique class that induce the biggest norm of the operator  $\mathcal{M}_{f}$  in the class  $\mathcal{S}$  for any  $\alpha>0$ . However, we find that there are other univalent functions  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  such that (7.5) still holds for any  $\alpha>-1$ .
We consider again the functions  $\mathcal{E}_{2}$  and  $P_{3}$ . We will check that
Proposition 7.28.
For each  $\alpha>-1$ ,
$\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)=\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.$
Proof of Proposition 7.28.
Recall that
$S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(z)=-\frac{3}{2}\frac{1}{(1-z)^{2}},\,S_{P_{3}}(z)=\frac{-2-4z^{2}}{(1-z^{2})^{2}},\,z\in\Delta.$
Then, for any  $z\in\Delta$ ,
$|S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(z)|\leq|S_{\kappa}(z)|,\,{\text{and}}\,\,|S_{P_{3}}(z)|\leq|S_{\kappa}(z)|=\frac{6}{|1-z^{2}|^{2}}.$
Hence we see that  $\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$ , and  $\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  for any  $\alpha>-1$ .
Next, we first show that  $\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(\alpha)\geq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$ . For  $\gamma>0$ , we have
(7.7)
$\frac{1}{(1-z)^{\gamma}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+\gamma)}{n!\Gamma(\gamma)}z^{n},z\in\Delta.$
Here  $\Gamma$  is the usual Gamma function, see [4]. For any  $\phi=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}\in\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)$ , we have
(7.8)
$\|\phi\|_{\alpha}^{2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n!\Gamma(\alpha+2)}{\Gamma(n+\alpha+2)}|a_{n}|^{2}.$
Let  $r\in(0,1)$  and  $2\lambda>\alpha+2$ . Then, from (7.7) and (7.8), we obtain that
(7.9)
$\|{(1-rz)^{-\lambda}}\|_{\alpha}^{2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n!\Gamma(\alpha+2)}{\Gamma(n+\alpha+2)}\Big|\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda)}{n!\Gamma(\lambda)}\Big|^{2}r^{2n}.$
By Stirling’s formula, we have
$\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda)}{n!}=(n+1)^{\lambda-1}[1+o(1)],\,\,{\textup{as}}\,\,n\rightarrow\infty.$
Here and later, we use  $o(1)$  to denote the general term of a sequence with  $o(1)\rightarrow 0,\,{\textup{as}}\,\,n\rightarrow\infty$ , which may be different in different places. Consequently, it follows from (7.9) that
(7.10)
$\displaystyle\|{(1-rz)^{-\lambda}}\|_{\alpha}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}{(n+1)^{\alpha+1}}[1+o(1)]\cdot\frac{(n+1)^{2\lambda-2}}{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}\cdot{(n+1)^{2\lambda-\alpha-3}}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+2)\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}.$
On the other hand, when  $2\lambda>\alpha+2$ , we have
(7.11)
$\displaystyle[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle=1+[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}\cdot[o(1)]\cdot r^{2n}.$
Note that  $o(1):=b_{n}\rightarrow 0,\,{\textup{as}}\,\,n\rightarrow\infty$  in (7.11). Then, for any small  $\varepsilon>0$ , there are two constants  $n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $c_{0}>0$  such that  $|b_{n}|\leq\varepsilon$  for  $n>n_{0}$  and  $|b_{n}|\leq c_{0}$  for all  $n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ .
It follows that
(7.12)
$\displaystyle[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}\cdot[o(1)]\cdot r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\leq[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]c_{0}\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\quad\quad\qquad+\varepsilon[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n={{n_{0}}+1}}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\leq c_{0}[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}+\varepsilon.$
Meanwhile,
(7.13)
$\displaystyle[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}\cdot[o(1)]\cdot r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\geq-[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}|b_{n}|r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\quad\quad\qquad-\varepsilon[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n={{n_{0}}+1}}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}r^{2n}$
$\displaystyle\geq-[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{n_{0}}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}|b_{n}|-\varepsilon.$
Combining (7.12) and (7.13), we obtain that
$\displaystyle[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}\cdot[o(1)]\cdot r^{2n}\rightarrow 0,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
so that
$\displaystyle[{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}}]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}\to 1,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
This means that
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{n!\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}[1+o(1)]r^{2n}=\frac{1+\hat{o}(1)}{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}},\,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Here and later,  $\hat{o}(1)$  denotes a function with respect to  $r$  with  $\hat{o}(1)\rightarrow 0,\,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$  which may be different in different places. Then, we obtain from (7.10) that, for  $2\lambda>\alpha+2$ ,
$\|{(1-rz)^{-\lambda}}\|_{\alpha}^{2}=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+2)\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{1+\hat{o}(1)}{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}},\,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Since
$\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}\neq 0,\phi\in\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)}\frac{\|S_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}(rz)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}}{\|\phi(z)\|_{\alpha}^{2}}$
for any  $r\in(0,1)$ , see [54, Page 1631], hence, by taking  $\phi(z)=(1-rz)^{-\lambda}$ , we obtain that, for  $2\lambda>\alpha+2$ ,
$\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\sup_{r\in(0,1)}\frac{9}{4}\frac{\|(1-rz)^{-\lambda-2}\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}}{\|(1-rz)^{-\lambda}\|_{\alpha}^{2}}$
$\displaystyle\geq\frac{9}{4}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+6)}{[\Gamma(\lambda+2)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}=\frac{9(\alpha+2)(\alpha+3)(\alpha+4)(\alpha+5)}{4[\lambda(\lambda+1)]^{2}}.$
Let  $\lambda\rightarrow{(\frac{\alpha}{2}+1)}^{+}$ , we get that
$\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.$
Now, we prove  $\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}(\alpha)\geq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$ . First, for  $r\in(0,1)$  and  $2\lambda>\alpha+2$ , similarly as above, we get that
$\|{(1-rz^{2})^{-\lambda}}\|_{\alpha}^{2}=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+2)\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{2^{\alpha+1}[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{1+\hat{o}(1)}{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}},\,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-},$
and
$\displaystyle S_{P_{3}}(\sqrt{r}z)(1-rz^{2})^{-\lambda}$
$\displaystyle=-2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda+2)}{n!\Gamma(\lambda+2)}r^{n}z^{2n}-4\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda+2)}{n!\Gamma(\lambda+2)}r^{n+1}z^{2n+2}$
$\displaystyle=-2-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\Big[2\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda+3)}{(n+1)!\Gamma(\lambda+2)}+4\frac{\Gamma(n+\lambda+2)}{n!\Gamma(\lambda+2)}\Big]r^{n+1}z^{2n+2}.$
Then, from (7.8) and by using similar arguments above, we obtain that
$\|S_{P_{3}}(\sqrt{r}z)(1-rz^{2})^{-\lambda}\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}=36\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+6)\Gamma(2\lambda-\alpha-2)}{2^{\alpha+5}[\Gamma(\lambda+2)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{1+\hat{o}(1)}{(1-r^{2})^{2\lambda-\alpha-2}},\,{\textup{as}}\,\,r\rightarrow 1^{-}.$
Consequently,
$\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\sup_{r\in(0,1)}\frac{\|S_{P_{3}}(\sqrt{r}z)(1-rz^{2})^{-\lambda}\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}}{\|(1-rz^{2})^{-\lambda}\|_{\alpha}^{2}}$
$\displaystyle\geq 36\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+6)}{2^{4}[\Gamma(\lambda+2)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}=\frac{9(\alpha+2)(\alpha+3)(\alpha+4)(\alpha+5)}{4[\lambda(\lambda+1)]^{2}}.$
Let  $\lambda\rightarrow{(\frac{\alpha}{2}+1)}^{+}$ , we obtain that
$\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.$
This finishes the proof of Proposition 7.28.
∎
We continue to investigate the properties of  $\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|$ . Let  $\alpha>-1$ , we define the functional  $\Lambda_{\alpha}$  as
$\Lambda_{\alpha}:S_{f}\mapsto\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha),\,\,f\in\mathcal{S}.$
We obtain that
Proposition 7.29.
For any fixed  $\alpha>-1$ ,  $\Lambda_{\alpha}$  is continuous on  $\overline{\mathbf{S}}$ , the closure of  ${\mathbf{S}}$ .
Proof.
Let  $\varepsilon>0$  be small. For  $f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{S}$  with  $S_{f_{1}},S_{f_{2}}\in\overline{\mathbf{S}}$ , we assume that  $\|S_{f_{1}}-S_{f_{2}}\|_{E_{2}}=\varepsilon$  so that
$|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{2}\leq\varepsilon,$
for all  $z\in\Delta$ . Then,
$\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|S_{f_{1}}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)+S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\||[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)|+|S_{f_{2}}(z)\phi(z)|\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}+\|S_{f_{2}}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\quad\qquad\qquad+(\alpha+5)\iint_{\Delta}2|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)||S_{f_{2}}(z)||\phi(z)|^{2}(1-|z|^{2})^{\alpha+4}\frac{dxdy}{\pi}.$
Note that, for  $\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1$ ,
$\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}\leq{\varepsilon}^{2}\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1},$
and
$(\alpha+5)\iint_{\Delta}2|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)||S_{f_{2}}(z)||\phi(z)|^{2}(1-|z|^{2})^{\alpha+4}\frac{dxdy}{\pi}\leq 12\varepsilon\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}.$
It follows that
$\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{f_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)+{\varepsilon}^{2}\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}+12\varepsilon\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}.$
Similarly, we have
$\mathbb{M}_{f_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)+{\varepsilon}^{2}\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}+12\varepsilon\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}.$
Consequently, we obtain that
$\Big|\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)-\mathbb{M}_{f_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)\Big|\leq(12+\varepsilon)\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}\|S_{f_{1}}-S_{f_{2}}\|_{E_{2}}.$
This implies that  $\Lambda_{\alpha}$  is continuous on  $\overline{\mathbf{S}}$ . The proposition is proved.
∎
For  $\alpha>-1$ , we define
${\mathbb{M}}(\alpha):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}}\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}}\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).$
Then we have
Proposition 7.30.
For each  $\alpha>-1$ , we have  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)<\mathbb{M}(\alpha)$  for any  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}$ .
Proof.
Let  $f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}$ . If  $\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=0$ , then  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)=0$  and the proposition holds. Next we will assume that  $\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}>0$  so that  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>0$ . Then we know from a classical result of the theory of universal Teichmüller space (see [3], [28]) that there is a constant  $\delta>0$  such that  $\mathcal{O}_{f}:=\{\varphi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\|\varphi-S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}<\delta\}$  is contained in  ${\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$ , here,  ${\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$  is defined as in (7.1). It follows that there is a function  $f_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}$  such that  $S_{f_{0}}=(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})S_{f}$  since  $(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})S_{f}$  belongs to  $\mathcal{O}_{f}$ . Then
$\mathbb{M}_{f_{0}}(\alpha)=(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).$
The proof of Proposition 7.30 is complete.
∎
Remark 7.31.
Proposition 7.29 and 7.30 suggest us that, for each  $\alpha>-1$ , if the biggest norm  $\mathbb{M}(\alpha)$  can be attained at some point  $S_{f}$  in  $\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$ , the closure of  $\mathbf{S}_{Q}$ , then  $S_{f}$  must lie on  $\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}$ . However, we do not know the answer to the following problem.
Problem 7.32.
Can the functional  $\Lambda_{\alpha}$  attain at least one maximum in  $\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{Q}$  for each  $\alpha>-1$ ?
Remark 7.33.
In light of Proposition 7.26, to find more functions satisfying the Brennan conjecture, it is natural to study the problem that in which subset of  $\mathcal{S}$  the Koebe function and its rotations provide the biggest norm for the multiplication operator when  $\alpha>0$ . That is
Problem 7.34.
For each  $\alpha>0$ , which functions  $f\in\mathcal{S}$  satisfy  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$ ?
It should be pointed out that it has been checked in [38] that for a large class of univalent functions  $f$  belonging to  $\mathcal{S}_{Q}$ ,  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  holds for each  $\alpha>0$ .
Remark 7.35.
Let  $\alpha>0,f\in\mathcal{S}$ . By checking carefully the arguments in the proof of Proposition  $8$  in [54, Page 1632], we see that, if there is a constant  $\varepsilon>0$  such that
$\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)+\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha+2)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)+\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha+2),$
for  $\alpha\in(0,\varepsilon)$ , then  $\beta_{f}({-2})\leq 1$ . Moreover, for  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  that have at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ , if there are two small constants  $\epsilon>0,\eta>0$  such that  $\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)<\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)-\eta$
for  $\alpha\in(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\cup(2-\epsilon,2+\epsilon)$ , then we will obtain that  $\beta_{R}(-2)<1$ , which is a contradiction. This leads us to conjecture that the following claim holds. Indeed, this is the case, and a proof of this claim can be found in [40].
Claim 7.36.
For each  $\alpha>-1$ , we have  $\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)\geq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  for all  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  that have at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ .
Remark 7.37.
We have proved that, for each  $\alpha>-1$ ,
$\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{2}(\alpha)=\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.$
It is interesting to consider the following
Problem 7.38.
For each  $\alpha>-1$ , which functions  $f\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  satisfy  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$ ?
Remark 7.39.
If our guess that Problem 7.34 has an affirmative answer for every  $f$  in  $\mathcal{S}$  is true, i.e.,  $\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  holds for every  $\alpha>0$  and all  $f\in\mathcal{S}$ , then the Brennan conjecture follows. Furthermore, since Claim 7.36 holds, it follows that  $\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)$  for every  $\alpha>0$  and all  $R\in\mathcal{U}_{R}$  that have at least one critical point on  $\mathbb{T}$ . Although these predictions may seem surprising, no counterexamples are known to the author. Finally, based on the above findings, we further conjecture that
Conjecture 7.40.
For every  $\alpha>0$ , if the functional  $\Lambda_{\alpha}$  attains the maximum on  $S_{f}$  in  $\overline{\mathbf{S}}$  for some  $f\in\mathcal{S}$ , then  $\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=6$ .
